Where a capability does not exist yet, the relevant section says so explicitly using one of: IMPLEMENTED · TESTED · VALIDATED · OPERATIONAL · PARTIAL · PLANNED · BLOCKED · DEPRECATED · UNKNOWN · NOT IMPLEMENTED · UNVERIFIED. Vocabulary discipline enforced throughout: never "confirmed" — only "candidate", "candidate event", "exocomet-like morphology", "candidate consistent with an exocomet interpretation". No numeric claim appears without source/method/date, or it's UNVERIFIED.

docs.title: 0.4 Terminology
docs.text:
Definitions below match how this codebase uses each term, not a generic textbook definition. Source: src/exocomet/core/types.py and src/exocomet/core/interfaces.py unless noted.

  • Exocomet — a comet-like body orbiting a star other than the Sun. Detected here only indirectly, via a dimming signature in that star's light curve, never imaged directly.
  • Transit — the passage of a body in front of its host star as seen from the observer, producing a temporary dip in measured brightness. In this codebase the term covers both planetary transits (for contrast) and the asymmetric dimming events attributed to a dust/gas tail (the object of the search).
  • Light curve — a time series of stellar brightness measurements. Represented in code by LightCurveData (core/types.py): target_id, mission, time (days, BKJD for Kepler / BTJD for TESS), flux (normalized so out-of-transit ≈ 1.0), flux_err, and a free-form meta dict carrying provenance (author/exptime, sectors/quarters used, detrending method, etc.).
  • Cadence — the sampling interval between consecutive light-curve points. Not a fixed constant in this codebase: LightCurveData.cadence_days is measured per light curve as the median of np.diff(time), because Kepler (29.4 min) and TESS (20 s–1800 s depending on product) differ by more than two orders of magnitude — see docs/research_log and Next Steps item A1 for why every window in config/thresholds.yaml is specified in days rather than a cadence count.
  • Detrending — dividing out slow instrumental/stellar trends before detection, implemented in detrend/detrend.py as either a Savitzky-Golay filter (detrend_savgol, the default) or a least-squares spline (detrend_spline).
  • Candidate (CandidateRecord, core/types.py) — one row of pipeline output: a detected DipEvent paired with its EventScore and, optionally, a VettingResult. A candidate is a pipeline output, not a claim about the sky.
  • Dip event (DipEvent) — a single detected dimming excursion: target, interpolated time and depth of minimum, its EventWindow, and (if both sides could be measured) an AsymmetryResult.
  • Detection — the act of Detector.detect() finding a DipEvent in a light curve. Distinct from flagging (EventScore.flagged), which is the pipeline's own decision that a detected event's shape is comet-like (see 05_detection_theory.md for the exact rule).
  • Candidate vs. confirmation — this document, and this project, never uses the word "confirmed" for a detection. A flagged event is a candidate, or a candidate consistent with an exocomet interpretation; confirming one requires follow-up (e.g. pixel-level vetting, spectroscopy, multi-epoch persistence) that this pipeline does not currently perform. The README states this explicitly under "Honest limitations."

docs.title: 0.5 Scope of this document
docs.text: This document (sections 0–10 and 35) covers document control, project foundation, scientific and astronomical background, the detection algorithm as implemented, data sourcing and storage architecture, software architecture, configuration, and a code-level reference for the io/ module. Sections 11 onward are being written by other contributors against the same repository state and are out of scope here.

docs.title: 1. Project Foundation
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 1.1 Project summary
docs.text: Exocomet Hunter is a Python framework (exocomet-hunter, src/exocomet/) for detecting comets orbiting other stars in NASA Kepler and TESS photometry. It is built and IMPLEMENTED for one concrete search — asymmetric, comet-like dimming events — and architected (via Detector/Vetter/Detrender/LightCurveSource abstract interfaces in core/interfaces.py) so a second kind of search can be added as a new class rather than a pipeline rewrite. Source: README.md, pyproject.toml description field ("A framework for detecting asymmetric, comet-like transit events in Kepler and TESS light curves").

docs.title: 1.2 The scientific problem
docs.text:
A planet is a solid, opaque disc: it covers and uncovers its star at the same rate, producing a transit that is symmetric in time and strictly periodic. A comet instead drags a tail of dust (and, closer to the star, gas) behind its nucleus. Two physical consequences follow:

  1. The transit is asymmetric — the compact, relatively opaque head blocks light quickly (steep ingress), while the more diffuse, extended tail clears more slowly (long egress).
  2. The transit is not periodic on any observable timescale — exocomets are inferred to be on long, eccentric orbits, so events recur irregularly if at all, with varying depths.

That asymmetry is the entire detection signal this project exploits. Section 4 (04_exocomet_physics.md) gives the physical picture in more detail and grounds it in the parametric model actually implemented in code; section 5 (05_detection_theory.md) gives the mathematics and the discriminating statistics.

docs.title: 1.3 The computational problem
docs.text:
Kepler alone measured ~200,000 stars' brightness every 29.4 minutes for four years; TESS covers most of the sky at multiple cadences (20 s–1800 s) across overlapping sectors. Two problems compound:

  • Scale. A full-sky search means searching hundreds of thousands of stars, each with tens of thousands of photometric points, for an event that individually looks like little more than a modest, temporary dimming.
  • Rarity and ambiguity. Genuine exocomet-like dips are rare, and the same asymmetric-dip shape can be produced by things that are not comets: stellar flares (opposite sign), eclipsing binaries (periodic), starspot rotation, and instrumental artefacts (thruster firings, thermal settling, sector/quarter boundaries). Distinguishing a real candidate from these is most of the engineering and statistical effort in this project (see docs/research_log/ for concrete, resolved instances of this problem).

Measured performance addressing the scale problem (README, §"Does it work?"): full-mission processing of one Kepler star (65,000 cadences, four years) takes 0.8 s. Source: README.md; per the Findings Log (2026-09-13), this was measured, not estimated, on the author's own machine (Apple M4, 10 cores). UNVERIFIED against an independent environment or a later code version — no CI benchmark currently reproduces this number (see 35_code_reference gaps and Next Steps item E7, "Benchmarks — not yet built").

docs.title: 1.4 Proposed solution
docs.text: An asymmetric-dip detection framework: detrend a light curve, flag statistically significant local dimmings, fit two competing parametric shapes (a symmetric Gaussian and a Gaussian-ingress/exponential-egress "comet" profile) to each one, and rank/flag by a combination of Bayesian model comparison (ΔBIC) and the fitted tail-to-core ratio τ/σ. This is IMPLEMENTED as AsymmetricDipDetector (detect/comet_detector.py), the first and — as of this commit — only concrete subclass of the Detector ABC (core/interfaces.py). See section 5 for the full mechanism and section 9 for the architecture that makes it a "first implementation" rather than the only possible one.

docs.title: 1.5 Core research question
docs.text: Stated in the project's own terms (README, Findings Log): can an independent-method, statistically characterised search recover known exocomet transit signatures in Kepler data, and can its own detection sensitivity be measured well enough to say what it would have missed? This is explicitly not framed as a discovery hunt — see 1.7 below.

docs.title: 1.6 Objectives
docs.text:
Primary (scientific/technical): - Recover previously published exocomet transit epochs in Kepler data as a validation gate, before trusting any result from a blind search. IMPLEMENTED and TESTED: AsymmetricDipDetector recovers all six dips reported by Rappaport et al. (2018) for KIC 3542116, within 0.184 d of the published epoch in the worst case (README; cross-checked in docs/research_log/003 and 006). Automated via scripts/run_validation.py / exocomet validate (Next Steps B6, done 2026-09-15). - Quantify detection sensitivity via injection-recovery, not just report a raw detection count. PARTIAL: calibration/injection.py exists and the README quotes a 50% floor near 750 ppm and 100% recovery above 1000 ppm from 200 synthetic injections — but Next Steps item B8 flags these specific numbers as stale, measured before the A1 (cadence-in-days) and A4 (ΔBIC+τ/σ flagging rule) fixes landed, and not yet re-measured. Treat the README's injection numbers as UNVERIFIED against the current code version until B8 is closed.

Secondary (methodological): - Rank candidates by a shape statistic that is actually diagnostic of comet-like asymmetry rather than one that merely detects "not symmetric." Resolved via research log 007 — see 05_detection_theory.md. - Build toward a trained classifier (Next Steps PART C) to eventually replace the hand-set ΔBIC/τ/σ flagging rule. PLANNED/PARTIAL: scripts/generate_training_labels.py and scripts/train_classifier.py exist; per Next Steps, the classifier's live-data backtest step is not fully verified (hung during testing, root cause the same class of MAST timeout issue documented elsewhere in this project).

Engineering: - Stream-and-discard photometry rather than mirroring the archive locally (§1.7, §7, §8). - A resumable, crash-safe ingestion pipeline able to run inside a bounded GitHub Actions budget and be killed at any point without losing completed work. IMPLEMENTED: scripts/ingest.py, io/ledger.py. Per Next Steps, "proven end-to-end on GitHub's own infrastructure... every step succeeds except the final push, which needs DATA_REPO_TOKEN" — i.e. BLOCKED on a credential the automated pipeline does not yet have, as of the date in this document's Status line.

Scientific extensions (not yet built): cross-mission validation, a physically-motivated comet light-curve simulator, a second independent detector, debris-disc vs. control population comparison. All PLANNED — see Next Steps PART F.

docs.title: 1.7 Scope and non-scope
docs.text:
In scope / actually implemented: - Single-star, single-method asymmetric-dip detection on Kepler and TESS light curves fetched from MAST. - Statistical characterisation of that one method's sensitivity via synthetic injection. - A resumable batch-ingestion pipeline with an append-only ledger and a disposable local SQLite query view.

Explicitly out of scope, and why (README, "Honest limitations"; Next Steps): - No pixel-level vetting. vetting/__init__.py is currently an empty module (module docstring only: "Catalogue cross-matching and false-positive checks."). NOT IMPLEMENTED. A background eclipsing binary bleeding into the photometric aperture cannot currently be excluded. Flagged as the single biggest missing capability by two independent external reviews recorded in the project's own Next Steps (item J1). - No confirmed discoveries. This project's vocabulary intentionally stops at "candidate" (§0.4). Confirmation requires follow-up (e.g. pixel-level analysis, independent-instrument corroboration) this pipeline does not provide. - No trials-factor correction. Per-event significance is not corrected for the number of places searched; the look-elsewhere effect applies to any blind search using this tool. PLANNED (Next Steps D5, J2 — an empirical look-elsewhere measurement via time-reversed/null light curves). - Not positioned as a discovery hunt. Kepler has already been searched, including a 2025 neural-network search of all 201,820 stars (README). This project positions itself as an independent-method cross-check with characterised sensitivity, explicitly not a claim to find something a prior search missed. - SIMBAD/Gaia cross-matching — mentioned as a data source in the README's "Data sources" section, but NOT IMPLEMENTED in code as of this commit (vetting/__init__.py is empty; no SIMBAD/Gaia query exists anywhere in src/exocomet/). See 06_data_sources.md.

docs.title: 1.8 Expected outputs
docs.text:
• Per-target candidate tables (CandidateRecord.to_row(), core/types.py) — one row per detected dimming event with its geometry, asymmetry, model-comparison, and (if run) vetting outcome.
  • An append-only processing ledger (io/ledger.py) and a disposable SQLite view over it (scripts/build_local_db.py) for ad-hoc querying of what has been processed and what was found.
  • Research-log write-ups (docs/research_log/) documenting real findings, including negative or partial results (e.g. the depth-offset investigation, 006, explicitly closes with "not resolved").
  • A planned but not-yet-built trained classifier, dashboard, and case-file export (Next Steps PART C, H2, J9) — all PLANNED, none IMPLEMENTED as of this commit.

docs.title: 1.9 Project philosophy
docs.text: Atharva Joshi's own stated preference, recorded in the project's Next Steps document (item H5): build-first. The project has been built and iterated aggressively — with a documented practice of testing claims against real data and reversing course when a hypothesis fails (e.g. three separate falsified hypotheses in research log 003; three tested and only partially confirmatory hypotheses in research log 006) — with a deferred, still-owed "learning pass": a plain-language walkthrough of every module so the author can explain every design choice himself, independent of who or what wrote the code originally. That learning pass is itself listed as PLANNED, not done, in Next Steps as of this document's date.

docs.title: 2. Scientific Motivation
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 2.1 Why search for exocomets
docs.text:
Comets in our own Solar System are considered relics of planet formation: icy, volatile-rich planetesimals left over from the outer disc that never accreted into a planet. Their dynamical activity — sublimation, tail formation, occasional disruption — is direct, ongoing evidence of processes that shaped the Solar System. An exocomet is the same kind of body, orbiting another star, inferred not by direct imaging (which is not feasible for a kilometre-scale nucleus at interstellar distances with current instruments) but from its effect on the host star's light: a transient dimming as its dust (and, near periastron, gas) tail crosses the line of sight, and in some systems, variable absorption features in high-resolution spectroscopy. This project only pursues the photometric (light-curve) signature.

Exocomets matter to several open questions in planet formation and system evolution:

  • Small-body populations and volatile delivery. Comets are candidate carriers of water and other volatiles to inner planets, in our own system and by analogy in others. A population of exocomets around debris-disc stars is direct evidence that this same class of body and process exists elsewhere.
  • Debris-disc dynamics. Stars with known debris discs (the leftover-planetesimal belt a comet would be dislodged from) are the physically motivated place to look for exocomet activity — not a random draw across all stars, but a targeted search of systems with a plausible reservoir. scripts/build_target_list.py and the seed lists in config/watchlist.txt / config/tess_training_hosts.txt are built on exactly this reasoning (both files' own comments: "chosen because infalling-comet activity is already established or plausible... not at random").
  • Planetary-system evolution over time. A star's small-body population evolves as planets form, migrate, and dynamically stir surrounding material; exocomet activity is one observable trace of that history.

docs.title: 2.2 Existing exocomet evidence
docs.text:
• β Pictoris — the canonical exocomet system, first inferred from decades of variable, redshifted absorption features (not photometric dips) attributed to infalling evaporating bodies. Included in this project's own target lists (config/watchlist.txt, config/tess_training_hosts.txt) as the "canonical exocomet system."
  • 49 Ceti, HR 4796, Fomalhaut, Vega, AU Mic, HD 181327, η Crv, HD 172555, RZ Psc — bright, well-characterised debris-disc or unusually variable young systems, also carried in the same watchlists as targets where infalling-body or comet-like activity is already established or considered plausible.
  • KIC 3542116 — the project's primary validation target. Rappaport et al. (2018, MNRAS 474, 1453; arXiv:1708.06069) reported six asymmetric, comet-shaped dips in Kepler photometry of this F2V star: steep ingress followed by a slower egress, aperiodic, depths of order 0.05–0.19% (491–1900 ppm), durations of order a day. This is the specific published result this pipeline is validated against (README, config/validation_targets.yaml, research logs 003 and 006). All six are recovered by AsymmetricDipDetector; see 05_detection_theory.md and 01_project_foundation.md §1.6 for details and caveats (notably the ~78% depth-recovery offset, research log 006, still open).
  • KIC 11084727 — a secondary Rappaport et al. (2018) target with one reported comet-shaped transit. Carried in config/validation_targets.yaml but its epoch has not been transcribed into that file (dips: [], with an explicit comment noting the omission) — this validation target is therefore currently inert; exocomet validate skips it with a printed SKIP line (cli.py, cmd_validate) rather than silently passing or failing it. NOT IMPLEMENTED / open item (Next Steps B5).

docs.title: 2.3 Research gap and where this project sits
docs.text:
The README states directly: "Kepler has been searched exhaustively, including a 2025 neural-network search of all 201,820 stars." Given that, this project explicitly positions itself as "an independent-method cross-check with characterised sensitivity," not a discovery hunt (README, "Honest limitations"). Two things distinguish that framing from simply re-running a known search:

  1. A different detection method. Rather than a trained neural network searching for a learned pattern, this pipeline uses an explicit, interpretable parametric model (a two-profile fit compared by ΔBIC, described in 05_detection_theory.md) whose failure modes can be individually diagnosed — as demonstrated by the project's own research log, which found and fixed two distinct, non-obvious statistical errors in its own primary discriminator (research logs 003 and 007) rather than treating the detector as a black box.
  2. Measured, not assumed, sensitivity. The project's stated goal is to report and characterise what its method would miss (injection-recovery completeness), rather than reporting a bare detection count. As noted in §1.6, the specific completeness numbers currently quoted in the README are flagged in the project's own Next Steps as stale and due for re-measurement (item B8) — the commitment to measuring sensitivity is real and structural (the injection-recovery harness exists and is exercised by exocomet inject), but the specific published numbers should be treated as UNVERIFIED against the current code version until that re-measurement happens.

Kennedy et al. (2019, MNRAS 482, 5587; arXiv:1811.03102), "An automated search for transiting exocomets," is cited in the README as prior work establishing the general two-profile (symmetric vs. asymmetric) model-comparison approach this project's own detect/model_comparison.py follows (see that module's own docstring, quoted in 05_detection_theory.md). This project does not claim methodological novelty over that prior work; its own framing is a from-scratch, independently-built implementation of the same class of approach, validated against a different published result (Rappaport et al. 2018) than Kennedy et al. themselves used.

docs.title: 3. Astronomical Foundations
docs.text:
Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

This section is deliberately brief: it exists to give a reader unfamiliar with time-domain photometry enough foundation to follow sections 4–6, not to be a general astronomy reference.

docs.title: 3.1 Light curves
docs.text: A light curve is a time series of a star's measured brightness (flux), typically normalised so its out-of-transit level is close to 1.0 — this is exactly the convention LightCurveData.flux follows in this codebase (core/types.py: "Flux normalised so that the out-of-transit level is approximately 1.0"). Space-based photometric surveys such as Kepler and TESS produce light curves by repeatedly measuring the same star's brightness at a fixed cadence over months to years, which is what makes it possible to catch a transient event lasting on the order of a day.

docs.title: 3.2 Transits, generally
docs.text: Any body passing in front of a star as seen from the observer produces a transit: a temporary reduction in measured flux. The shape of that reduction over time — how quickly it darkens, how deep it gets, how it recovers — encodes information about the transiting body's size, opacity structure, and orbital geometry. The two transit shapes this project's science is built around (a solid opaque disc vs. a comet nucleus-plus-tail) are described in detail in section 4; the underlying general point is that transit shape, not merely transit existence, is diagnostic of what caused it.

docs.title: 3.3 Why space-based photometry from Kepler/TESS enables this search
docs.text: Ground-based photometry cannot achieve the combination of precision, cadence, and multi-year time baseline needed to catch and characterise dips as shallow as ~0.05–0.19% (491–1900 ppm, the depths reported for KIC 3542116 by Rappaport et al. 2018) lasting about a day, repeated irregularly over years. Kepler's four-year, nearly-continuous 29.4-minute-cadence monitoring of ~200,000 stars, and TESS's near-all-sky coverage at cadences from 20 s to 1800 s depending on data product, are what make catching and statistically characterising events at this depth and duration feasible at all. Section 6 (06_data_sources.md) covers the specific mission and data-product details this codebase relies on.

docs.title: 4. Exocomet Physics
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 4.1 Nucleus, coma, dust tail, gas tail
docs.text:
A comet is a small (kilometre-scale), volatile-rich body. As it approaches its star, solar/stellar heating sublimates surface ices, releasing gas and entrained dust that form a coma around the nucleus and are swept by radiation pressure and stellar wind into a trailing tail — generally a dust tail (curved, following the orbital path) and, closer in, a gas/ion tail (more nearly radially aligned with the star). None of this physical structure is separately modelled in this codebase — no nucleus/coma/tail geometry, optical depth, or orbital-dynamics simulation exists in src/exocomet/ as of this commit. NOT IMPLEMENTED. What is implemented is a photometric consequence of this structure: an asymmetric, extended obscuration profile, described below and modelled directly as a parametric light-curve shape rather than derived from a physical dust-tail simulation.

A physically-grounded forward model (nucleus/tail geometry, optical depth, orbital velocity, limb darkening → simulated light curve) is explicitly PLANNED, not built: Next Steps item F2 and its sharper restatement J5 both describe this as the single highest-leverage improvement to the project's training data, precisely because the current injected/fitted shapes (described below) are a piecewise-empirical stand-in for it, not a physical simulation.

docs.title: 4.2 Transit geometry: impact parameter and duration
docs.text: The general transit-geometry concepts — impact parameter (how centrally the transiting body crosses the stellar disc) and transit duration (set by orbital velocity, stellar radius, and impact parameter) — apply to an exocomet transit as they do to any transit, but this codebase does not model them explicitly as physical parameters. DipEvent.window (core/types.py, an EventWindow) records only the empirical start/end index and time of a detected dip, and event duration is read directly off the light curve (EventWindow.duration_days), not derived from an orbital/geometric model. Impact parameter is not represented anywhere in the codebase. NOT IMPLEMENTED as a physical quantity; what exists is the empirical geometric measurement only.

docs.title: 4.3 Dust-tail geometry and optical depth: the model actually implemented
docs.text:
The photometric model this project fits — and the one all of section 5's discussion of shape statistics is built on — lives in src/exocomet/detect/model_comparison.py. Its module docstring states the physical motivation directly:

"Comet — a Gaussian ingress joined at the minimum to an exponential egress. This is the standard optically-thin dust-tail parameterisation: the obscuration builds as the head approaches and then decays as the tail sweeps out."

This is an optically-thin approximation: the model does not represent a spatially resolved dust column with its own optical-depth profile; it represents the net fractional flux loss over time as a two-piece analytic curve. Concretely (comet_profile, model_comparison.py):

  • Ingress (falling side, t ≤ t0): flux = baseline − depth · exp(−½((t − t0)/σ)²) — a Gaussian, parameterised by ingress_width (σ, in days). This represents the compact, relatively opaque head/nucleus region blocking light as it approaches conjunction.
  • Egress (rising side, t > t0): flux = baseline − depth · exp(−(t − t0)/τ) — an exponential decay, parameterised by egress_tau (τ, in days). This represents the more extended, progressively less opaque trailing dust tail clearing the line of sight.

The two halves are joined continuously at the minimum t0, both reaching baseline − depth there (comet_profile docstring: "The two halves meet continuously at the minimum, both reaching baseline - depth there"). depth is the fractional flux loss at minimum; baseline is the local out-of-dip flux level. A lower bound of 1.0e-4 days (_MIN_WIDTH_DAYS) is applied to both σ and τ during fitting, purely to prevent the optimiser from collapsing either width onto a single cadence — this is a numerical safeguard, not a physical claim about minimum tail width.

For contrast, the competing symmetric model (symmetric_profile) is a single Gaussian with one shared width parameter on both sides — the shape expected from a solid, opaque, disc-shaped occulter (a planet) or from ordinary noise/artefact excursions. Section 5 covers how the two are compared.

docs.title: 4.4 The photometric signature: depth, symmetry, and long egress
docs.text:
The observable signature can be framed this way, consistent with the code above:

  • Flux reduction / depth. For the primary validation target, KIC 3542116, published depths span 491–1900 ppm (0.05%–0.19% of the star's brightness); per-measurement noise in that star after detrending is ~83 ppm, so even the deepest published event is only ~23× the noise of a single measurement (Findings Log, 2026-09-13).
  • Symmetry vs. asymmetry. A planet's transit is symmetric because the same opaque, fixed-size disc covers and uncovers the star at the same rate. An exocomet's transit is asymmetric because the head (compact, more opaque) and the tail (extended, less opaque, still clearing after the head has passed) are physically different structures with different obscuration timescales — the fast-fade/slow-recovery pattern the comet_profile Gaussian-ingress/exponential-egress shape is built to capture.
  • Long egress as the diagnostic feature. The physically meaningful statement, in this project's own terms, is τ/σ > 1: an egress timescale (τ) longer than the ingress width (σ) indicates a trailing tail — obscuration that clears more slowly than it accumulated. ModelComparison.tau_over_sigma (core/types.py) is the code's direct implementation of this ratio. Section 5 (05_detection_theory.md) covers why this fitted-profile ratio, rather than a simpler duration comparison at a fixed depth level, is the statistic this project actually uses to decide whether an event is comet-shaped.

docs.title: 4.5 What is explicitly not modelled here
docs.text: To be direct about the gap between the physical picture in §4.1 and the implemented model in §4.3: this project's comet_profile is a phenomenological curve fit chosen because it matches the qualitative fast-fade/slow-recovery shape and is analytically tractable to fit by least squares — it is not derived from first-principles dust-tail radiative transfer, orbital mechanics, or an assumed tail composition/density profile. The gap between "a curve shaped like what we expect" and "a curve derived from comet physics" is exactly what Next Steps items F2/J5 (a physical forward simulator) are meant to close, and it is currently open. PLANNED, NOT IMPLEMENTED.

docs.title: 5. Detection Theory
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. IMPLEMENTED and TESTED against the KIC 3542116 validation set unless noted otherwise.

docs.title: 5.1 Planetary transit vs. exocomet transit: the discrimination problem
docs.text: As established in section 4, a planetary transit is symmetric and strictly periodic; an exocomet transit is asymmetric (fast fade, slow recovery) and not periodic on any observable timescale. Section 5 covers how this codebase turns that qualitative distinction into a quantitative, testable decision rule — and documents two real, project-specific findings (research logs 003 and 007) about how that rule can fail in non-obvious ways even when it appears to be working.

docs.title: 5.2 The mathematical signal model, as implemented
docs.text:
Two competing profiles are fit to every detected event (detect/model_comparison.py):

Symmetric (symmetric_profile, the null hypothesis — describes a planet, an eclipsing binary, or a symmetric noise excursion equally well):

flux(t) = baseline − depth · exp(−½((t − t0)/width)²)

Parameters: t0 (time of minimum), depth, width (a single Gaussian σ shared by both sides), baseline.

Comet (comet_profile — Gaussian ingress joined to an exponential egress at the minimum):

flux(t) = baseline − depth · exp(−½((t − t0)/ingress_width)²)   for t ≤ t0
flux(t) = baseline − depth · exp(−(t − t0)/egress_tau)          for t > t0

Parameters: t0, depth, ingress_width (σ), egress_tau (τ), baseline — one more free parameter than the symmetric model.

Both are fit by bounded nonlinear least squares (scipy.optimize.least_squares, method "trf", up to 2000 function evaluations) over a window widened by padding_factor (default 1.5×) beyond the detected event window, specifically so the recovering tail — which by construction extends past the point where flux first returns within the detection threshold — is not truncated (compare_models docstring). Each fit is packaged as a ModelFit (core/types.py) carrying chi2, n_params, n_points, and a converged flag; ModelFit.bic computes chi2 + n_params · ln(n_points) (lower is better), with the n_params penalty specifically there to stop the comet model's extra free parameter from winning by flexibility alone (docstring: "The penalty term is what stops the extra free parameter of the comet profile from winning by flexibility alone").

compare_models returns None — an explicit "not fit" outcome, not a fabricated number — when the padded window holds fewer than 8 cadences, too few to constrain the 5-parameter comet model.

docs.title: 5.3 Shape parameters, by their real names in the code
docs.text:
Symbol (science note / research log) Code name (ModelFit.params key) Meaning σ ingress_width (comet model) / width (symmetric model) Gaussian standard deviation of the falling side, days τ egress_tau E-folding timescale of the recovering side, days — depth Fractional flux loss at minimum — t0 Time of minimum — baseline Local out-of-dip flux level

ModelComparison.tau_over_sigma (core/types.py) computes egress_tau / ingress_width directly from the fitted comet-model parameters, returning nan if either is non-finite or ingress_width ≤ 0.

docs.title: 5.4 ΔBIC: the model-comparison ranking statistic
docs.text: ModelComparison.delta_bic (core/types.py) is BIC(symmetric) − BIC(comet); positive favours the comet profile. ModelComparison.favors_comet returns True when delta_bic exceeds a configured threshold (ScoringConfig.delta_bic_threshold, default 10.0 in config/thresholds.yaml — the conventional "strong evidence" cutoff per Kass & Raftery 1995, cited in research log 007's references). This threshold is a single source of truth: it is passed into ModelComparison at construction from ScoringConfig.delta_bic_threshold specifically "so there is one source of truth" between the ranking metric and the flagging decision (core/types.py comment on ModelComparison.delta_bic_threshold).

docs.title: 5.5 τ/σ: why it matters, and what it alone cannot tell you
docs.text:
ΔBIC answers "is this profile asymmetric relative to a symmetric model?" It does not answer "is the asymmetry pointed in the direction a trailing dust tail produces?" — a fast-fade/slow-recover event and its exact time-reversed mirror image (slow fade, fast recovery — a leading-tail or otherwise "backwards" geometry, unphysical for a trailing comet tail) are equally asymmetric relative to a symmetric model, so ΔBIC cannot distinguish them. Only τ/σ carries directional information: τ/σ > 1 means the fitted egress is longer than the fitted ingress — the trailing-tail signature; τ/σ < 1 means the reverse.

This is not a hypothetical concern — it is a documented, resolved bug in this project's own history. Research log 007 (docs/research_log/007-delta-bic-is-direction-blind.md) constructed a synthetic mirror-image test: two events, identical in depth, noise, and total duration, differing only in which side was the long one.

Trailing tail (comet-like) Leading tail (time-reversed) ingress / egress duration 2.4 h / 12.0 h 12.0 h / 2.4 h τ/σ 4.15 0.23 ΔBIC 151 201 (higher)

The physically backwards event scored a higher ΔBIC than the genuine comet-like event. On ΔBIC alone, the unphysical event would have been the more confident detection. This is why the actual flagging rule (detect/scoring.py, score_event) requires both conditions:

flagged = (
    np.isfinite(delta_bic) and np.isfinite(tau_over_sigma)
    and delta_bic > cfg.delta_bic_threshold
    and tau_over_sigma > cfg.tau_over_sigma_threshold
)

with ScoringConfig.tau_over_sigma_threshold defaulting to 1.0. Research log 007's explicit warning: "Do not 'simplify' this rule by dropping the τ/σ condition." Doing so would silently readmit every physically-backwards event the fix was written to exclude, without failing the six-dip validation gate (both real comet events and their hypothetical mirror images pass ΔBIC identically well) — the same failure mode as research log 003, arriving from a different direction (see §5.6).

docs.title: 5.6 The half-depth comparison problem (research log 003)
docs.text:
Before τ/σ existed as the primary shape statistic, this project's original discriminator was a contour-based duration asymmetry, A_dur = (T_egress − T_ingress) / (T_egress + T_ingress), with each side's duration measured from the half-depth crossing to the dip minimum (detect/asymmetry.py, measure_side / compute_asymmetry — this code and metric still exist and are still computed and reported, just no longer used to decide flagging; see below).

The problem, found empirically 2026-09-13: running the detector on KIC 3542116 recovered all six published dips, but the measured A_dur values were inconsistent and mostly negative, even though Rappaport et al. (2018) describe every one of these events as having a steeper ingress and a longer egress — every value should have been positive.

Three hypotheses were tested and eliminated (research log 003): baseline window too short (falsified — sweeping 101→1001 cadences moved A_dur by <0.02); detrending distorting the profile (falsified — raw and detrended flux gave identical values); sign convention inverted in code (falsified — synthetic injections with known ordering recovered the correct sign).

The actual cause is mathematical, not a coding error. At depth fraction f, the Gaussian ingress side reaches the contour at T_ingress(f) = σ√(2 ln(1/f)) and the exponential egress side at T_egress(f) = τ ln(1/f). At the half-depth contour (f = 0.5) these become 1.177σ and 0.693τ respectively. Setting them equal gives the sign-change condition:

τ/σ = 1.177 / 0.693 ≈ 1.70

So any event with a genuinely longer tail in the range 1 < τ/σ < 1.70 — a real, physically comet-like event — produces a negative half-depth A_dur, the wrong sign, because the half-depth contour samples the compact, nearly-symmetric core of the profile, not the extended wing where the comet signature actually lives (core/types.py, ModelComparison.tau_over_sigma docstring, and research log 003 both state this explicitly). Confirming evidence: measuring A_dur at successively deeper contours (50% → 25% → 12.5% depth) moved every one of the six dips monotonically toward positive, exactly as this explanation predicts (research log 003's table).

Resolution: ModelComparison.tau_over_sigma, derived from the whole fitted profile rather than a single depth-fraction level set, became the primary shape statistic, with ΔBIC as the primary ranking metric (§5.4–5.5). A_dur (and its bootstrap significance, EventScore.a_dur_sigma/significance) is retained in EventScore and CandidateRecord.to_row() as a reported, interpretable cross-check — but per detect/scoring.py's own docstring, it "no longer decide[s]" whether an event is flagged.

Wider lesson, stated directly in the research log and worth repeating here: the pipeline recovered 6/6 published epochs while its central discriminator carried the wrong sign. Recovering known events at the right time is necessary but not sufficient — it says nothing about whether the shape statistic driving a classification decision is even pointed the right direction. This is why this project treats "passes the validation gate" and "the discriminating statistic is trustworthy" as two separate claims, each requiring its own evidence (research logs 003 and 007 are the record of that evidence for the statistics currently in use).

docs.title: 5.7 The full decision sequence (README, detect/comet_detector.py)
docs.text:
1. Detrend — remove instrumental drift (detrend/detrend.py; see 07_data_architecture.md).
  2. Find candidates — flag runs of cadences ≥4σ (config: CandidateConfig.sigma_threshold) below a rolling-median baseline using a robust MAD-based noise estimate (detect/candidates.py, detect/baseline.py).
  3. Measure shape — locate the interpolated minimum, measure ingress/egress duration and slope at the half-depth crossing (detect/asymmetry.py).
  4. Fit and compare models — symmetric vs. comet profile, ranked by ΔBIC (§5.2–5.4).
  5. Quantify uncertainty — bootstrap A_dur by perturbing in-event flux within its error bars and re-measuring (detect/scoring.py, bootstrap_a_dur_sigma, default 1000 draws).
  6. Flag — delta_bic > threshold AND tau_over_sigma > threshold (§5.5).
  7. Vet — PLANNED/NOT IMPLEMENTED. vetting/__init__.py is currently empty; no automated cross-check against variable-star/eclipsing-binary catalogues, flare morphology, or cross-target artefact detection exists in code yet, despite being described in the README's own numbered list of pipeline steps. See 06_data_sources.md §6.4 and Next Steps item D2.

A periodicity check (detect/scoring.py, periodicity_flag, Lomb-Scargle via astropy.timeseries) is also computed per light curve and reported on EventScore.periodic/period_days, used as a ranking penalty, "never as a hard rejection" (docstring) — i.e. it does not gate flagged.

docs.title: 6. Data Sources
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 6.1 NASA Kepler and TESS
docs.text:
Kepler. Long-cadence photometry at 29.4 minutes. This exact figure is load-bearing in this codebase: Next Steps item A1 ("Window sizes are counted in measurements, not in time," ✅ done 2026-09-14) records that every window in config/thresholds.yaml was originally chosen in units of Kepler long-cadence measurements, and had to be converted to physical time (days) once TESS data — sampled at wildly different rates — entered the pipeline. LightCurveData.cadence_days (core/types.py) is measured per light curve, not assumed, as the median of np.diff(time).

TESS. SPOC pipeline products at 120 s (the standard 2-minute cadence) and 20 s; Full-Frame-Image (FFI)-derived products at 200 s, 600 s, and 1800 s depending on which TESS extended-mission phase produced them. Verified directly against real MAST queries during the A1 investigation: at 120 s cadence, the (then Kepler-tuned) 401-cadence detrend window worked out to 13.4 hours; at 20 s cadence, the same 401-cadence window was only 2.2 hours — both far too short relative to the ~1-day comet dips this project is looking for, which is exactly what motivated converting every window to a days-based config (DetrendConfig.window_days, BaselineConfig.median_window_days, etc. — see 10_configuration.md).

Both missions are accessed exclusively through the single io/download.py module — "Only this module knows about lightkurve" (module docstring) — so the rest of the pipeline operates on LightCurveData without caring which mission or pipeline produced it.

docs.title: 6.2 MAST, and how io/download.py actually queries it
docs.text:
fetch_light_curve (io/download.py) wraps lightkurve.search_lightcurve(...).download_all(...).stitch(). Two real, documented problems and their fixes govern how this query is actually constructed (both closed under Next Steps item A2, "TESS products from different pipelines get stitched together," ✅ done 2026-09-14):

Author/exptime pinning. A plain lk.search_lightcurve(target, mission="TESS") can return dozens of products from different pipelines (QLP, SPOC, TARS, TASOC, TESS-SPOC, TGLC) at cadences from 20 s to 1800 s. Blindly stitching all of them caused two distinct real problems (found and fixed 2026-09-14, per the module's own "Notes" docstring on fetch_light_curve): (1) a detrending/baseline window sized for one cadence is a wildly wrong physical duration at another; (2) at least one HLSP pipeline (TARS) reports flux as an already zero-centred residual rather than raw counts, so stitching it in could divide by a near-zero median and corrupt normalisation outright. The fix: fetch_light_curve now defaults to author="SPOC", exptime=120 for TESS and author="Kepler" for Kepler/K2, pinning to a single pipeline rather than only separating by cadence. Verified against real data (Next Steps A2): β Pic resolved to 10 clean SPOC/120s products, down from 54 mixed-pipeline products, with flux normalising to a sane 0.99–1.01 range.

Bounded network calls. Every MAST call (search_lightcurve, download_all) runs on a daemon thread with an explicit wall-clock timeout (DEFAULT_SEARCH_TIMEOUT=60s, DEFAULT_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT=300s) and bounded retries (DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3, exponential backoff from DEFAULT_RETRY_BACKOFF=5s), raising MastTimeoutError (subclasses TimeoutError) rather than blocking indefinitely. The module docstring records why this exists as a hard requirement, not a nicety: "a fetch for KIC 3542116 sat at zero CPU for nine minutes and had to be killed, twice," even though the underlying files had already fully downloaded — the process was blocked on a socket with no deadline. A related, separately-fixed bug: a retry against a poisoned local cache (a FITS file left truncated by an earlier interrupted download) would fail identically every time unless the corrupt cache entry was cleaned up between attempts — _call_with_retries's cleanup callback exists specifically for this (see 35_code_reference/io.md for the exact mechanism).

Stream-and-discard. discard_after_read=True deletes the cached mastDownload tree for a target immediately after its arrays are extracted, so the local working set stays at a few megabytes regardless of how many stars are processed (README: "Light curves are streamed and discarded by default"). This exact behaviour was, for a period, a silent no-op — see 07_data_architecture.md §7.3 and 08_storage.md for the specific bug and fix (Findings Log, 2026-09-14).

docs.title: 6.3 NASA Exoplanet Archive and VizieR
docs.text:
VizieR is IMPLEMENTED as a real query target: scripts/build_target_list.py pulls a published, vetted debris-disc catalogue — Cotten & Song (2016), ApJS 225, 15, VizieR id J/ApJS/225/15, "A Uniformly Vetted Compilation of Debris Disk Candidates" — chosen specifically because it is already literature-cross-checked rather than a raw infrared-excess catalogue needing its own vetting pass (script's own module docstring). It cross-matches each disc star's sky position against the TESS Input Catalog (astroquery.mast.Catalogs) to resolve TIC/KIC identifiers, confirms real downloadable photometry exists via the same lightkurve search machinery used elsewhere, and selects a magnitude-matched control star per disc star (for the planned debris-disc-vs-control comparison, Next Steps F4).

However, per Next Steps item 3 ("FIRST THING NEXT SESSION"), build_target_list.py's control-group matching is currently broken — "it queries VizieR/TIC for real and returns disc-star matches, but the matched-control step returns zero matches, so it produces no output files" — and its output is not yet wired into scripts/ingest.py's target sources. ingest.py currently runs against the 33 hardcoded seed targets (23 Kepler + 10 TESS) only (get_target_list(), scripts/ingest.py). PARTIAL.

NASA Exoplanet Archive is named in the README's "Data sources" list ("target and cross-match data from... the NASA Exoplanet Archive") but no code in src/exocomet/ or scripts/ queries it as of this commit. NOT IMPLEMENTED — this appears to be an aspirational/planned data source stated in the README rather than a currently-exercised one; readers should not assume Exoplanet Archive data has been cross-matched into any current target list or result.

docs.title: 6.4 SIMBAD and Gaia
docs.text:
Both are listed in the README's "Data sources" section ("Kepler/TESS photometry from MAST; target and cross-match data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive, VizieR, SIMBAD and the Gaia archive"). Neither is implemented. src/exocomet/vetting/__init__.py — the module that would house SIMBAD object-type lookups and Gaia stellar-parameter cross-matching, per Next Steps item D2's own description of the planned module contents (catalogs.py: "SIMBAD object type (astroquery.simbad), AAVSO VSX variable flag, Kepler/TESS eclipsing-binary catalogue membership, Gaia parameters") — currently contains only a module docstring and no functions, classes, or imports:

"""Catalogue cross-matching and false-positive checks."""

NOT IMPLEMENTED. No astroquery.simbad or Gaia-archive import exists anywhere in src/exocomet/. This is a real gap between the README's stated data sources and the current code, not a subtle distinction — anyone relying on this document to understand what vetting has actually run against a candidate should read this as: no catalogue cross-match vetting has been performed on any candidate this pipeline has produced, as of this commit.

docs.title: 7. Data Architecture
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 7.1 FITS file structure as lightkurve/astropy deliver it
docs.text: Raw photometry arrives as FITS files fetched by lightkurve.search_lightcurve(...).download_all(...). This codebase does not parse FITS structure directly — no astropy.io.fits calls appear anywhere in src/exocomet/; all FITS handling is delegated to lightkurve, which returns a LightCurveCollection that this project immediately .stitch()es into one combined lightkurve.LightCurve object before ever touching its own types. io/download.py's module docstring states this design choice directly: "Only this module knows about lightkurve... everything downstream operates on LightCurveData... so the science code neither knows nor cares where the photometry came from." Consequently, this document does not attempt to describe Kepler/TESS FITS extension layout (e.g. LIGHTCURVE/APERTURE HDUs) — that structure is entirely internal to lightkurve and never surfaces past _to_light_curve_data (io/download.py).

docs.title: 7.2 The fields this codebase actually reads
docs.text:
_to_light_curve_data (io/download.py) pulls exactly three arrays off the stitched lightkurve object — lc.time.value, lc.flux.value, lc.flux_err.value — and constructs LightCurveData (core/types.py) from them:

LightCurveData field Type Meaning target_id str Catalogue identifier, e.g. "KIC 3542116" mission str "Kepler", "K2", or "TESS" time float64 array Days; BKJD for Kepler, BTJD for TESS flux float64 array Normalised so out-of-transit ≈ 1.0 flux_err float64 array Per-cadence uncertainty, same normalised units as flux meta dict[str, Any] Free-form provenance (see below)

Quality flags are not retained as a separate array. lightkurve's download_all(..., quality_bitmask=quality_bitmask) call applies a quality mask during the download step (default "default", meaning cadences the mission pipeline flagged as bad are already removed before lightkurve hands back the light curve) — but the underlying per-cadence quality bitmask itself is never carried into LightCurveData. Downstream code cannot ask "was this specific cadence flagged, and for what reason" — only "was it already excluded by the mask applied at download time." This is a real, load-bearing gap: any candidate event should be understood as having survived whatever quality_bitmask="default" excludes, and nothing more granular is currently recorded or queryable. NOT IMPLEMENTED as a first-class field.

meta does carry real provenance, populated at two points: - _to_light_curve_data: n_dropped_nonfinite, n_dropped_duplicate_timestamp, median_raw_flux, source="MAST". - fetch_light_curve's extra_meta: n_products, author, exptime (None for non-TESS), sectors_or_quarters (best-effort extracted list of sector/quarter numbers actually used).

Cadences with non-finite time, flux, or flux_err are dropped outright (good = np.isfinite(time) & np.isfinite(flux) & np.isfinite(flux_err)), and duplicate timestamps (from overlapping quarters/sectors) are also dropped, with the count logged rather than silently discarded — the module docstring notes this is deliberate: "a large count here is itself a sign that mismatched products... got stitched together."

docs.title: 7.3 Temporary-data lifecycle: download → extract → delete
docs.text:
The canonical ordering is implemented in scripts/ingest.py's process_one_target, and its module docstring is explicit that the order is the safety mechanism, not a transaction:

  1. Fetch the light curve from MAST — raw FITS lands on local disk (data/raw/ by default), not yet deleted.
  2. Save the extract to disk, atomically (io/extract.save_extract, see 08_storage.md).
  3. Only now, delete the raw FITS (shutil.rmtree(raw_cache_dir / "mastDownload", ...)).
  4. Run the detection pipeline (detrend + detector) on the extract.
  5. Write the results file, atomically.
  6. Only now, append one ledger line recording success.

If the process is killed anywhere before step 6, no ledger entry exists for that attempt, so the target is simply retried on the next run — steps 2 and 5 are each independently atomic (os.replace-based), so a killed run never leaves a half-written extract or results file, only, at worst, a missing one. This ordering is deliberately conservative about when raw FITS is deleted: discard_after_read=False is passed to fetch_light_curve inside process_one_target specifically so the FITS survives until after step 2 lands durably — the module docstring notes that deleting it as a side effect of fetch_light_curve itself (as discard_after_read=True does elsewhere) "would collapse steps 1 and 3 into one, removing the ordering guarantee this function exists to provide."

A real, previously-shipped bug in this exact lifecycle (Findings Log, 2026-09-14): discard_after_read=True's cleanup step (_discard_cached, io/download.py) originally matched a normalised slug of the catalogue target_id (e.g. "kic1161345") against downloaded cache directory names to decide what to delete. lightkurve names its cache directories after its own pipeline-internal identifiers, never the search string used — a Kepler product is kplr001161345_lc_... (no "kic" substring anywhere), and a TESS HLSP product embeds a zero-padded TIC number mid-filename, unrelated to a resolved common name like "beta Pic" (itself containing no digits at all). The slug never matched anything, for any target, on either mission — this had presumably been true since the function was first written, and was found only when data/raw/ was observed to have grown to 166 MB despite every download supposedly discarding after read. Fixed: _discard_cached now wipes the entire mastDownload tree under the cache directory rather than attempting to match subdirectories by name — correct as long as targets are processed one at a time, which is true of every current caller, but explicitly noted (in the function's own docstring) as needing per-target cache subdirectories once a parallel-worker batch (Next Steps E4) is built.

docs.title: 7.4 Data retention policy
docs.text:
Data Retained? Where Raw FITS No — deleted after extraction (§7.3) or immediately via discard_after_read=True in ad-hoc use data/raw/mastDownload/ (transient only) Extract (time/flux/flux_err + metadata) Yes — the permanent, detector-independent record of what was measured <data-repo-dir>/extract/<mission>/<target>.parquet (see 08_storage.md) Results (candidate events, one pipeline version's output) Yes <data-repo-dir>/results/<mission>/<target>.jsonl Processing ledger (append-only attempt log) Yes, indefinitely, append-only <data-repo-dir>/ledger.jsonl

This is a deliberate design decision, not an oversight: the archive (MAST) is public and permanent, so mirroring it locally is storage spent on something already guaranteed to exist (io/download.py module docstring). The Findings Log (2026-09-13) records the actual scale reasoning behind this: one Kepler star's full extract is ~7.7 MB and takes ~62 s to download (latency-dominated across ~18 separate files); a full Kepler-scale mirror (200k stars) would be roughly 1.5 TB and 1–3 weeks of downloading on the author's own connection, against only 24 GB of free local disk at the time — download, not compute, is the binding constraint, and it is a constraint the stream-and-discard architecture sidesteps entirely by never needing to hold more than one star's raw data at a time.

docs.title: 8. Storage
docs.text:
Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. All three layers below are IMPLEMENTED and covered by unit tests (tests/unit/test_extract.py, tests/unit/test_ledger.py, tests/unit/test_build_local_db.py).

The storage architecture has three layers, each with a distinct role: a permanent per-target extract (parquet), an append-only processing history (JSONL ledger), and a disposable queryable view rebuilt on demand (SQLite). None of the three is a second source of truth for another — each is described in its own module as being built from, not alongside, the layer beneath it.

docs.title: 8.1 Extract format — io/extract.py
docs.text:
Layout: <base_dir>/extract/<mission>/<sanitized target_id>.parquet, computed by extract_path(base_dir, mission, target_id). sanitize_target_id replaces spaces and path separators with underscores (e.g. "KIC 3542116" → "KIC_3542116") purely to produce a filesystem-safe name — the docstring is explicit that this is "not... reversible on its own," and that this is fine, because the original unsanitized target_id is always recovered from the file's own embedded metadata (below), never from the filename.

File contents. time, flux, flux_err become parquet columns (pa.float64()); target_id, mission, and meta (JSON-encoded) ride along as parquet file-level schema metadata, not a sidecar file — namespaced keys exocomet.target_id, exocomet.mission, exocomet.meta_json. The module docstring gives the reasoning: keeping everything in one file means "there is only ever one thing to write atomically and only one thing that can go missing or drift out of sync," at the cost of requiring meta to be JSON-serialisable (already true of every producer in this codebase). pyarrow is used directly (not pandas.DataFrame.to_parquet) because schema metadata does not reliably survive a pandas round trip.

Atomicity (save_extract). The table is written to a temporary file in the same directory as the final path (tempfile.mkstemp(..., dir=str(path.parent)), ensuring the later rename stays on one filesystem), then moved into place with os.replace, which is atomic on POSIX — covering both GitHub Actions runners and macOS, the two environments this pipeline runs on. A reader can therefore only ever observe the target path as either completely absent or completely written; there is no window where a half-written file is visible at the final name. If anything raises before the replace completes, the temporary file is removed in an exception handler so it can never be mistaken for a real, complete extract.

Round-trip guarantee (load_extract). Reconstructs target_id, mission, and meta from the schema metadata and the three columns from parquet; the docstring states the result "round-trips exactly: identical arrays (float64 in, float64 out, no precision loss from parquet) and an identical meta dict for any JSON-serializable input."

See 35_code_reference/io.md for full function signatures.

docs.title: 8.2 Append-only ledger — io/ledger.py
docs.text:
Purpose, and what it replaced. The ledger replaces an earlier pattern (results/processed_ledger.json, one JSON object rewritten whole at the end of a run) used by scripts/monitor_new_data.py. That pattern loses every completed record the instant the process is killed mid-run, because the previous good state exists only in memory until the final rewrite lands — unacceptable under a bounded (~30 minute) GitHub Actions budget where the runner can be killed at any moment. The ledger instead opens in "a" (append) mode and writes one JSON line per event, so a completed record is durable the moment append_entry returns — there is no whole-file rewrite step for a kill to interrupt.

LedgerEntry fields (@dataclass(frozen=True)): target_id, mission (together the key), status ("success" or "failed"), timestamp_utc (ISO-8601 UTC), attempt (1-indexed, set by the caller — the ledger does not independently track attempt counts), error (message on failure, None on success), extract_path, results_path (both None when not applicable, e.g. a failure before any output existed).

Durability mechanism (append_entry). After writing the JSON line, the function calls both handle.flush() (moves bytes out of Python's io buffer) and os.fsync(handle.fileno()) (forces them to the physical device) — the docstring is explicit that flush() alone is insufficient because the OS page cache can still hold the bytes indefinitely; fsync is what lets a record survive not just a killed Python process but a killed/rebooted runner.

Torn-write guard, both directions. Before writing, append_entry checks whether the ledger file's last byte is a newline; if not (a previous process was killed mid-write()), it emits a leading newline first, so the new entry cannot be glued onto the end of a broken prior line, turning one bad line into two. On read, read_ledger skips (and logs) any line that fails to parse as JSON, rather than raising — so a torn trailing line from an interrupted write never causes N−1 good, already-fsync'd records to be lost.

Derived views, all pure functions over the flat entry list: latest_entries (last entry per (target_id, mission)); get_status ("done" iff the latest entry for a key is status="success", otherwise "pending" — retryable failures and never-attempted targets are deliberately conflated here); next_targets (targets still needing processing: never-attempted first in input order, then retriable failures oldest-failure-first, excluding anything that has exhausted max_attempts or already succeeded).

docs.title: 8.3 Disposable local SQLite view — scripts/build_local_db.py
docs.text:
Explicitly not a second source of truth. The module docstring states this directly: "This script is not a second source of truth — it is a queryable view, rebuilt from scratch on demand, never committed to git, never written by CI." Every run deletes any existing --out file and rebuilds it fully from <data-repo-dir>/ledger.jsonl (and, for candidate counts, the results files the ledger points at) — a full rebuild is described as "cheap (well under a second)" given the ledger is one line per attempt across at most a few hundred targets, which the module argues avoids an entire class of incremental-sync bugs.

Three tables (_SCHEMA in build_local_db.py): - attempts — one row per raw ledger line, the full retry history: target_id, mission, status, timestamp_utc, attempt, error, extract_path, results_path. Nothing deduplicated. - targets — one row per (target_id, mission) (primary key), the latest-status view built from latest_entries: same columns as attempts plus retries_left (computed against --max-attempts, meaningful only when status='failed'), n_candidates, n_flagged. n_candidates/n_flagged are NULL, not 0, when results_path is unset or the file doesn't exist (failed or never-attempted target — nothing to count), and 0 when the results file exists but is empty (fully processed, zero detections). The docstring calls this NULL-vs-zero distinction deliberate — it is "the whole reason this table reads the results files at all rather than trusting the ledger alone." - candidates — one row per detected event, columns mirroring CandidateRecord.to_row() (target_id, t_min, depth_ppm, duration_days, a_dur_sigma, significance, delta_bic, tau_over_sigma, signs_agree, flagged, periodic, period_days, vetting_status, vetting_reasons) plus mission, foreign-keyed to targets.

Default output path is local.db in the current directory, deliberately not inside <data-repo-dir> — the docstring's reasoning: the data-repo directory is meant to be a git clone of the separate exocomet-hunter-data repository, and dropping a disposable, frequently-regenerated binary file inside it risks it being swept up by a stray git add -A there.

docs.title: 8.4 Data integrity: what is actually checked, and what is not
docs.text: Mechanism Status Atomic file replacement (os.replace) for extracts and results files IMPLEMENTED — io/extract.save_extract, scripts/ingest.py's _write_results_jsonl fsync-backed durability for ledger writes IMPLEMENTED — io/ledger.append_entry Torn-write recovery (corrupt last line) IMPLEMENTED — both the leading-newline guard on write and the skip-and-log behaviour on read, io/ledger.py Round-trip fidelity of extract arrays/metadata TESTED — load_extract/save_extract round-trip, asserted in tests/unit/test_extract.py per the module's own docstring claim Checksums on stored data (extracts, results) NOT IMPLEMENTED. No hash/checksum of extract or results file contents is computed or stored anywhere in io/extract.py, scripts/ingest.py, or the ledger schema. A silently corrupted (but structurally valid) parquet or JSONL file would not be detected by anything in this pipeline. Provenance manifest (config, code version, package versions, seed, target-list hash) PLANNED, NOT IMPLEMENTED as a general mechanism — Next Steps item E3. A narrower, already-built instance exists for the classifier only: scripts/train_classifier.py's models/manifest_<mission>.jsonl records row counts, class counts, host stars, date, package versions, and training-set hash — but this is specific to classifier training data, not a general per-run provenance record for detection runs.

docs.title: 9. Software Architecture
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 9.1 Design philosophy: framework over script
docs.text: Stated directly in the README: "The package is a framework, not a script." The concrete mechanism is a set of abstract interfaces in core/interfaces.py that the rest of the pipeline is written against, rather than against the exocomet detector specifically — the module's own docstring: "A different search — for example the planned anomalous-dimming (technosignature) detector — is added by implementing Detector and passing it to exocomet.pipeline.run_target; no orchestration code changes." (Note: exocomet.pipeline.run_target is the docstring's own forward reference to planned orchestration — see §9.5; it does not exist yet as of this commit.)

docs.title: 9.2 The four interfaces, with their real method signatures
docs.text:
All four live in src/exocomet/core/interfaces.py.

LightCurveSource (typing.Protocol, @runtime_checkable): 

def fetch(self, target_id: str, mission: str) -> LightCurveData: ...
Implemented by MastLightCurveSource (io/download.py).

Detrender (Protocol, @runtime_checkable): 

def detrend(self, lc: LightCurveData) -> LightCurveData: ...
Implemented by SavGolDetrender and SplineDetrender (detrend/detrend.py), each wrapping the corresponding module-level function (detrend_savgol, detrend_spline).

Vetter (Protocol, @runtime_checkable): 

def vet(self, event: DipEvent, lc: LightCurveData) -> VettingResult: ...
No concrete implementation exists. vetting/__init__.py is an empty module (docstring only). NOT IMPLEMENTED.

Detector (abc.ABC): 

class Detector(ABC):
    name: str = "detector"

    @abstractmethod
    def detect(self, lc: LightCurveData) -> list[DipEvent]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def score(self, event: DipEvent, lc: LightCurveData) -> EventScore: ...

    def run(self, lc: LightCurveData) -> list[CandidateRecord]:
        return [CandidateRecord(event=event, score=self.score(event, lc)) for event in self.detect(lc)]
The class docstring frames the split deliberately: "A detector answers two questions: which parts of a light curve look like events (detect), and how confident we are that a given event is real (score). Splitting the two keeps the expensive statistical work off the path of the cheap first pass." The base run() implementation is a naive detect-then-score loop; concrete subclasses may override it for efficiency (see §9.3 — AsymmetricDipDetector.run does exactly this).

docs.title: 9.3 The one concrete detector: AsymmetricDipDetector
docs.text:
detect/comet_detector.py. Its own module docstring states its scope precisely: "This class is deliberately thin. It owns no science of its own; it sequences the baseline estimation, candidate finding, geometric measurement and statistical scoring implemented in the sibling modules." Concretely:

  • baseline_and_noise(lc) — converts BaselineConfig.median_window_days/noise_window_days to cadence counts via days_to_cadences (using that light curve's own measured cadence_days) and calls rolling_baseline/local_noise (detect/baseline.py).
  • detect(lc) — calls find_candidate_events (detect/candidates.py) then measure_event (detect/asymmetry.py) per window. Events whose ingress or egress could not be fitted are still returned, carrying unmeasurable_reason, rather than silently vanishing.
  • score(event, lc) — recomputes the baseline (again, since score may be called independently of detect) and calls score_event (detect/scoring.py).
  • run(lc) — overrides the base Detector.run, computing the baseline and the Lomb-Scargle periodogram once per light curve rather than once per event, since both are properties of the whole series, not of one event. This is the method actually used by every real caller (cli.py, scripts/ingest.py).

A fixed RNG (np.random.default_rng(self.config.runtime.rng_seed), default seed 42) is instantiated once per detector instance and reused across the bootstrap significance draws in score_event, so results are reproducible run-to-run for identical input data and config.

docs.title: 9.4 Repository structure
docs.text:
src/exocomet/
  core/        — types.py, config.py, interfaces.py (no dependency on lightkurve/archive APIs)
  io/          — download.py (MAST only), extract.py (parquet), ledger.py (JSONL)
  detrend/     — detrend.py (Savitzky-Golay / spline)
  detect/      — baseline.py, candidates.py, asymmetry.py, model_comparison.py, scoring.py, comet_detector.py
  calibration/ — injection.py, features.py (synthetic injection-recovery, classifier features)
  vetting/     — empty (NOT IMPLEMENTED, see 09.2/09.5)
  viz/         — plots.py
  cli.py       — `exocomet` console script

scripts/       — ingest.py, build_local_db.py, build_target_list.py, build_kepler_host_list.py,
                 generate_training_labels.py, train_classifier.py, run_validation.py,
                 measure_depth_offset.py, monitor_new_data.py, vet_host_list.py
config/        — thresholds.yaml, validation_targets.yaml, watchlist.txt, tess_training_hosts.txt
docs/          — NEXT_STEPS.md, SESSION_LOG_*.md, research_log/, cloud-routine-prompt*.md, specification/ (this document)
tests/         — unit/, integration/, benchmarks/ (benchmarks currently an empty package, see Next Steps E7)
.github/workflows/ — ingest.yml, survey.yml (disabled), train.yml

pyproject.toml declares the package under src/ layout ([tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"]), Python ≥3.11, and a single console-script entry point exocomet = "exocomet.cli:main".

docs.title: 9.5 Future detector architecture: H4 (technosignature detector)
docs.text: Named directly in both the README ("the planned anomalous-dimming (technosignature) detector") and Next Steps item H4: "Project 2 — technosignature / anomalous dimming. New Detector subclass (Isolation Forest on light-curve features), validated on Boyajian's Star (KIC 8462852), reusing io/, detrend/, core/, vetting/." PLANNED. NOT IMPLEMENTED. No code toward this exists in src/exocomet/ as of this commit — it is cited here specifically because it is the concrete test case the Detector ABC's plugin design (§9.1–9.2) is meant to prove out: adding this detector should require writing one new class, not modifying core/, io/, or detrend/. Whether that claim holds has not yet been tested, since H4 has not been attempted.

docs.title: 10. Configuration
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. IMPLEMENTED and TESTED (config loading is exercised by unit tests across detect/, detrend/, and cli.py tests).

docs.title: 10.1 config/thresholds.yaml, field by field
docs.text:
The file's own header comment states its purpose: "Every number the detection pipeline depends on lives here rather than being hardcoded, so that each choice can be cited, justified in the methodology write-up, and varied in sensitivity tests without touching code." All values below are the actual shipped defaults as of this commit.

detrend — Savitzky-Golay window controls: - window_days: 8.1871 — must be far longer than the longest expected dip so real events survive detrending. Chosen to be exactly equivalent to the previous Kepler-only window_length=401 (long-cadence) count, preserved specifically so pre-A1 validation results did not move when the units changed from cadences to days. - polyorder: 2 - upper_sigma_clip: 5.0 — points this far above the trend are clipped before fitting; downward excursions (the signal being searched for) are never clipped. - spline_knot_spacing_days: 1.5 — used only by the alternative spline detrender (detrend_spline), kept for a detrending-method comparison, not the default path.

baseline — rolling-median reference level and robust noise: - median_window_days: 2.0621, noise_window_days: 2.0621 — both exactly equivalent to the previous median_window=101 (Kepler long cadence).

candidates — what counts as a candidate dip (detect/candidates.py): - sigma_threshold: 4.0 — a cadence is "in dip" at 4σ below baseline (robust, MAD-based sigma). - min_consecutive: 3 — rejects single-cadence cosmic-ray hits. - max_gap_cadences: 2 — in-dip runs separated by at most this many cadences are merged. - max_window_days: 3.0 — hard cap so a long instrumental excursion cannot grow an unbounded window. - recovery_sigma: 1.0 — window edges extend outward until flux recovers to within this many sigma of baseline. - edge_margin_days: 1.0208 — events entirely within this many days of either end of the series are discarded (truncated-window baseline/noise estimates are noisier there, and sector/quarter boundaries are a known artefact source); exactly equivalent to the previous edge_margin_cadences=50.

asymmetry (detect/asymmetry.py): - half_depth_fraction: 0.5 — the depth fraction at which ingress/egress duration is measured for the (now reported-only) A_dur statistic. See 05_detection_theory.md §5.6 for why this specific choice is the source of the half-depth sign-flip problem. - min_points_per_side: 3 — a side below this cadence count is marked unmeasurable rather than scored on noise. - (search_padding_factor: 2.0 is a dataclass default in core/config.py's AsymmetryConfig and does not currently appear as its own line in thresholds.yaml; the YAML file only overrides half_depth_fraction and min_points_per_side for this section, everything else in AsymmetryConfig falls back to its Python-level default.)

scoring — the flagging decision (detect/scoring.py; see 05_detection_theory.md §5.4–5.5 for the physics/statistics reasoning): - bootstrap_draws: 1000 - significance_threshold: 3.0 — |A_dur|/σ(A_dur) required to call an event "significantly asymmetric" by the old contour statistic; reported, not decisive. - require_sign_agreement: true — reported field on AsymmetryResult/EventScore, not itself gating flagged (the actual gate is the two conditions below). - delta_bic_threshold: 10.0 — the conventional "strong evidence" BIC-difference cutoff. - tau_over_sigma_threshold: 1.0 — trailing-tail requirement. - periodicity_min_period_days: 0.5, periodicity_max_period_days: 50.0 — Lomb-Scargle search range. - periodicity_fap_threshold: 0.01 — false-alarm-probability cutoff below which a periodogram peak is treated as a genuine periodic signal (used as a ranking penalty only, per 05_detection_theory.md §5.7).

search: target_batch_size: 40, shortlist_size: 20 — batch-search sizing, consumed by scripts/build_target_list.py/related batch tooling.

runtime: rng_seed: 42 (threaded through every stochastic step, e.g. the bootstrap in score_event, for reproducibility), max_workers: null (documented as meaning os.cpu_count() - 1; PARTIAL — no code in src/exocomet/ currently reads or applies max_workers to spawn a worker pool, so this field is not yet consumed anywhere as of this commit; parallel batch processing is Next Steps item E4, PLANNED).

docs.title: 10.2 config/validation_targets.yaml
docs.text:
Header comment states the intent directly: "The pipeline must recover these before any result from the blind search is trusted." match_tolerance_days: 0.5 — deliberately far looser than the paper's own quoted ±0.02 d epoch uncertainty, because this pipeline reports the flux minimum, which need not coincide exactly with the paper's fitted epoch.

Two targets are defined: - KIC 3542116 (Kepler; Rappaport et al. 2018) — expected_dip_count: 6, with all six epochs (BKJD) and published depths transcribed from the paper's Table 3, each carrying a short note (e.g. "D140, shallow", "D1268, deep"). This is the primary, fully-active validation target. - KIC 11084727 (Kepler; same paper) — expected_dip_count: 1, but dips: [], with an explicit comment: "Epoch not yet transcribed... Read it from the paper before enabling this target in the validation gate." Inert as of this commit (Next Steps B5, open); exocomet validate (cli.py, cmd_validate) prints SKIP for a target with no transcribed dips rather than silently passing or failing it.

docs.title: 10.3 Typed configuration classes — core/config.py
docs.text:
Every YAML section above has a matching frozen dataclass: DetrendConfig, BaselineConfig, CandidateConfig, AsymmetryConfig, ScoringConfig, SearchConfig, RuntimeConfig, composed into one PipelineConfig. Loading is strict, not permissive:

  • PipelineConfig.from_yaml(path) reads the YAML and delegates to from_dict.
  • PipelineConfig.from_dict(raw) iterates every dataclass field of PipelineConfig, and for each section: if the YAML supplies unknown keys not present on the corresponding dataclass, it raises ValueError("unknown key(s) in config section '<name>': [...]"). This means a typo in thresholds.yaml fails loudly at load time rather than being silently ignored.
  • A section or key omitted entirely from the YAML falls back to the dataclass's own Python-level default (this is how AsymmetryConfig.search_padding_factor, noted above, currently resolves — it is not in the YAML, so the code default of 2.0 applies).
  • PipelineConfig.to_dict() serialises the full effective configuration (via dataclasses.asdict) — intended for run manifests and logging, though as noted in 08_storage.md, no general per-run provenance manifest currently consumes this (Next Steps E3, PLANNED).

Module docstring: "Defaults here mirror config/thresholds.yaml so that an installed copy of the package works without the repository checked out." This is a maintained invariant, not automatically enforced — the values were manually kept in agreement as of this commit (verified directly above; DetrendConfig.window_days = 8.1871 etc. match the YAML exactly), but there is no test asserting the dataclass defaults and the shipped YAML never drift apart. UNVERIFIED as an automated guarantee.

docs.title: 10.4 Parameter overrides via the CLI
docs.text: exocomet run, exocomet validate, and exocomet inject (cli.py) all accept --config PATH, loaded via _load_config, which calls PipelineConfig.from_yaml(path) if a path is given, else falls back to PipelineConfig() (all built-in defaults). There is no per-field CLI override (e.g. no --sigma-threshold flag) — the only override mechanism is supplying a complete or partial YAML file matching the shape of thresholds.yaml. scripts/ingest.py's run_ingest accepts the same --config pattern independently (its own config_path parameter, defaulting to built-in PipelineConfig() when not given).

docs.title: 11. Pipeline Overview
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16. Git HEAD is commit 01c2051. The working tree at the time this was written also carries uncommitted changes to scripts/ingest.py and scripts/build_kepler_host_list.py (verified via git diff) that fix a live bug found the same day; this section describes the code as it currently sits on disk, and calls out the uncommitted status explicitly wherever it matters. IMPLEMENTED / TESTED (offline unit tests) / OPERATIONAL (one real GitHub Actions run confirmed end-to-end, verified live against AJpro-merc/exocomet-hunter-data).

docs.title: 11.1 What "the pipeline" means here
docs.text:
There are two related things called "the pipeline" in this codebase and it matters which one a given section is about:
