  1. The detection pipeline — detrend → find candidates → measure asymmetry → score (detrend_savgol, find_candidate_events, measure_event, score_event). Pure computation on an in-memory LightCurveData; no I/O of its own. See 12_acquisition.md through 17_uncertainty.md.
  2. The ingestion pipeline (scripts/ingest.py) — the resumable, hourly-run orchestration that fetches a target, runs the detection pipeline on it, and durably records the outcome. This section is about the ingestion pipeline.

docs.title: 11.2 The six-step per-target sequence
docs.text:
scripts/ingest.py's process_one_target() (lines 214–316) performs exactly six steps, in this order, per the module's own docstring (lines 9–24):

  1. Fetch the light curve from MAST (exocomet.io.download.fetch_light_curve). Raw FITS files land on local disk; nothing is deleted yet.
  2. Save the extract to disk, atomically (exocomet.io.extract.save_extract) — the permanent, detector-independent time/flux/flux_err arrays as a parquet file at extract/<mission>/<target>.parquet.
  3. Only now, delete the raw FITS (shutil.rmtree(raw_cache_dir / "mastDownload", ...)).
  4. Run the existing detection pipeline (detrend_savgol then AsymmetricDipDetector(config).run(detrended)) on the extract.
  5. Write the results file, atomically (_write_results_jsonl), one JSON line per CandidateRecord.to_row(), at results/<mission>/<target>.jsonl. Written even when there are zero candidates — an empty file is retained as meaningful evidence that the star was processed and found quiet, distinct from "never attempted."
  6. Only now, append one ledger line recording success (exocomet.io.ledger.append_entry, status="success").

docs.title: 11.3 Why this exact order is the safety mechanism
docs.text:
Quoting the module docstring directly (scripts/ingest.py lines 19–24):

If the process is killed anywhere before step 6, no ledger entry exists for this attempt, so the target is simply retried next run — save_extract and the results write are both themselves atomic, so a killed run never leaves a half-written extract or results file behind, only (at worst) a missing one. The ledger line is written last, deliberately, so it can never claim success for work that did not fully land.

This was a real design decision, not an incidental ordering choice, driven by the GitHub Actions execution environment: ingest.yml runs on a 45-minute timeout-minutes budget and the runner can be killed by GitHub at any point with no graceful-shutdown guarantee. run_ingest() checks the time budget once per target, at the top of the loop (gating whether to start another target, never interrupting one already in flight) — a star is the atomic unit of work.

Concrete failure mode this ordering prevents: if the ledger were written before detection ran (or before the extract was durably saved), a runner killed mid-detection would leave a ledger entry claiming status="success" for a target with no results file and possibly no extract — a permanent, silent lie in the source of truth that no later run would ever notice or correct, because next_targets() (see 11.5) would treat that target as done.

Both save_extract (io/extract.py lines 82–125) and _write_results_jsonl (scripts/ingest.py lines 188–211) achieve their own atomicity the same way: write to a temporary file in the same directory, then os.replace() into the final path (atomic on POSIX, which covers both GitHub Actions runners and macOS). A reader can therefore only ever observe the final path as completely absent or completely written.

docs.title: 11.4 A real, verified bug this ordering did not prevent (but a nearby check did)
docs.text:
Session Log 2026-09-15 §11 records a live-tested failure mode: process_one_target printed "1 succeeded" but the extract file was missing from disk afterward on the first real MAST test. Root cause traced to _call_with_retries (io/download.py) retrying download_all against a poisoned local cache with no cleanup between attempts — not a bug in the six-step ordering itself, but in a lower layer. Two fixes landed as a result: _call_with_retries gained a cleanup callback wired to _discard_cached() between attempts (io/download.py lines 161–207, 412), and ingest.py added a belt-and-braces immediate readback check right after save_extract (lines 268–274) — a ledger entry claiming success for output that is not actually on disk is treated as unreachable-but-checked-anyway, per the code comment:

a ledger entry claiming success for a file that isn't actually there is a worse failure mode than a loud, immediate one, so it's checked directly rather than trusted.

docs.title: 11.5 Failure recovery: the ledger's resume logic
docs.text:
State lives entirely in <data-repo-dir>/ledger.jsonl, an append-only JSON-lines file (exocomet.io.ledger). Two functions drive resumability:

  • latest_entries(entries) (lines 165–177) — reduces the full, chronological ledger to one entry per (target_id, mission) key: the last entry seen wins. This is "current status per target."
  • next_targets(ledger_path, all_targets, mission, max_attempts=3) (lines 197–241) — returns exactly the targets that still need processing:
  • Never-attempted targets, in the order given in all_targets — first, so a bounded run spends its budget on fresh ground before retries.
  • Then retriable failures (status="failed" and attempt < max_attempts), oldest-failure-first by timestamp_utc — so one flaky target being retried repeatedly cannot starve an older failure.
  • Excluded entirely: targets whose latest entry is status="success", or whose latest entry is status="failed" with attempt >= max_attempts (exhausted).

run_ingest() (scripts/ingest.py lines 318–421) calls next_targets() at the start of each mission's run, then processes targets[:max_targets] within the time budget. On any exception, it writes a status="failed" ledger entry and continues to the next target — one bad star never kills the run (except Exception as exc: # noqa: BLE001, line 382).

docs.title: 11.6 The 2026-09-16 permanent-failure fix (uncommitted at time of writing)
docs.text:
This is the live bug referenced by the task brief, and it is present in the working tree but not yet in git history (git status shows scripts/ingest.py and scripts/build_kepler_host_list.py as modified, uncommitted, on top of 01c2051).

The bug: KEPLER_HOST_STARS (the hardcoded Kepler target tuple) previously contained five KIC identifiers — KIC 1571512, 3735741, 3839966, 4457741, 4569375 — that do not correspond to any real Kepler observation. Session Log 2026-09-15 §9 already notes the list "was never checked against a real catalog when it was hand-curated" (the same root cause as the earlier KIC 1026032 removal). fetch_light_curve() raises FileNotFoundError for such a target (io/download.py lines 392–396, "no products for this target"). Before the fix, run_ingest()'s exception handler recorded this the same way as any other failure — one ledger entry per attempt, attempt incremented each time — so next_targets() kept re-selecting these five targets on every hourly run until max_attempts (default 3) was reached, burning the whole per-run target budget on targets that can never succeed, and (because the kepler job's failure blocked the sequenced tess job via needs: kepler in ingest.yml) skipping TESS ingestion entirely. gh run list (see 23_automation.md) shows two real ingest runs failing this way six hours apart on 2026-09-16.

The fix (scripts/ingest.py lines 382–419, current working-tree state): the exception handler now distinguishes FileNotFoundError — "the MAST search itself returned zero results ... not a transient network issue" — from every other exception. When isinstance(exc, FileNotFoundError), the ledger entry is written with attempt=max_attempts immediately, in one entry rather than accumulating one per run, so next_targets() excludes the target from every subsequent run without needing three real attempts to get there. The five bad IDs were also removed outright from KEPLER_HOST_STARS (scripts/build_kepler_host_list.py, working tree), reducing the Kepler host list from ~23 to 18 targets; they were not added to KNOWN_BAD_HOSTS (which is reserved for stars with real data and a real astrophysical reason for exclusion, e.g. KIC 1026032's eclipsing binary) because they simply do not exist as observed Kepler targets.

docs.title: 11.7 Concurrency
docs.text: Two runs processing the same target simultaneously is prevented at the GitHub Actions level: ingest.yml sets concurrency: {group: ingest, cancel-in-progress: false}, which queues a second trigger rather than running it in parallel. There is no in-process lockfile in ingest.py itself — the module docstring states this is "simpler, and sufficient given the workflow already owns this guarantee."

docs.title: 11.8 What this section does not cover
docs.text:
• The survey.yml / scripts/monitor_new_data.py path is a separate, older, currently-disabled pipeline with its own results/processed_ledger.json state file (not the JSONL ledger described above). See 23_automation.md.
  • train.yml (classifier training) is a distinct, also-disabled workflow layered on top of the same exocomet-hunter-data repository. See 23_automation.md.

docs.title: 12. Data Acquisition
docs.text:
Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051 (this module is unmodified in the working tree's uncommitted diff). IMPLEMENTED / TESTED.

All light-curve retrieval from MAST is confined to one module, src/exocomet/io/download.py (581 lines). Its own docstring states the design intent directly: "Only this module knows about lightkurve. Everything downstream operates on LightCurveData, so the science code neither knows nor cares where the photometry came from."

docs.title: 12.1 Public surface
docs.text:
• fetch_light_curve(target_id, mission="Kepler", cadence="long", author=None, exptime=None, cache_dir=DEFAULT_CACHE_DIR, discard_after_read=False, quality_bitmask="default", search_timeout=60.0, download_timeout=300.0, max_attempts=3, retry_backoff=5.0) -> LightCurveData (lines 285–433) — download, stitch and normalise all available photometry for one target.
  • iter_light_curves(target_ids, ..., discard_after_read=True, skip_errors=True, per_target_timeout=900.0, ...) -> Iterator[LightCurveData] (lines 468–541) — yields light curves one at a time, discarding each after it is consumed; the memory- and disk-safe way to process a large target list.
  • MastLightCurveSource (lines 544–581) — a thin class wrapper satisfying the LightCurveSource protocol in core/interfaces.py, delegating to fetch_light_curve.
  • MastTimeoutError(TimeoutError) (lines 85–91) — raised when a MAST network call exceeds its wall-clock budget. Subclasses TimeoutError so existing except OSError / except Exception handlers keep working unchanged.

docs.title: 12.2 Target selection and pinning (the A2 fix)
docs.text:
fetch_light_curve pins a single pipeline (author) and, for TESS, a single exposure time (exptime), rather than accepting whatever lightkurve finds:

  • Kepler/K2: author defaults to "Kepler"; cadence ("long" or "short") is passed through.
  • TESS: author defaults to "SPOC", exptime defaults to 120 (seconds).

This exists because of a real, documented problem (module docstring, lines 353–364, "Next Steps A2"): a plain lk.search_lightcurve(target, mission="TESS") can return dozens of products from different pipelines (QLP, SPOC, TARS, TASOC, TESS-SPOC, TGLC, ...) at cadences from 20 s to 1800 s. Blindly stitching all of them together caused two distinct, separately-found problems:

  1. A detrending/baseline window sized for one cadence is a wildly wrong physical duration at another (see 13_detrending.md, A1).
  2. At least one HLSP pipeline (TARS) reports flux as an already zero-centered residual rather than raw counts, so stitching it in could divide by a near-zero median and corrupt the normalisation outright.

Pinning to a single author/exptime avoids both at once.

docs.title: 12.3 Timeout and retry behaviour (the 2026-09-15 hardening)
docs.text:
Before 2026-09-15, no MAST call in this module had a wall-clock bound. The module docstring records the concrete incident that motivated the change: a fetch for KIC 3542116 sat at zero CPU for nine minutes and had to be killed, twice, even though the 17 FITS files already in the cache were all complete and written within one minute — "the process was blocked on a socket that never returned and had no deadline to hit."

The fix layers three independent bounds:

  • _call_with_timeout(func, timeout, description) (lines 126–158) — runs func on a daemon thread and gives up waiting after timeout seconds, raising MastTimeoutError. A daemon thread is used deliberately, not concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor, because a stalled MAST socket cannot be cancelled from outside — the worker thread may still be alive when the caller stops waiting, and a daemon thread does not block interpreter exit the way a ThreadPoolExecutor (which joins its workers at shutdown) would. The documented honest limitation: this bounds how long the caller waits, not the orphaned thread's socket, which keeps holding it until astroquery's own timeout trips — which is why the next bound exists too.
  • _configure_astroquery(timeout=120.0, pagesize=5000) (lines 94–123) — pins astroquery.mast.conf.timeout/.pagesize and, best-effort, the private _portal_api_connection/_service_api_connection attributes (their names have moved across astroquery releases, so this degrades gracefully and never fails a download over it).
  • _call_with_retries(func, timeout, description, max_attempts=3, backoff=5.0, cleanup=None) (lines 161–207) — bounded retry (never infinite), exponential backoff (5 s, 10 s between attempts). The cleanup callback runs between failed attempts, added specifically because a download interrupted partway leaves a truncated FITS file cached on disk; simply calling download_all again does not fix it, because lightkurve finds the file already present at its cache path and does not know it is broken — "a retry with no cleanup is not actually a retry in that case, just the same failure repeated on a timer" (line 178–181). At the download_all call site this is wired to _discard_cached(cache, target_id).

Documented budgets (module-level constants, lines 52–80):

Constant Value Purpose DEFAULT_SEARCH_TIMEOUT 60.0 s catalogue query ceiling DEFAULT_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT 300.0 s bulk FITS fetch ceiling DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS 3 total attempts per network call (≤2 retries) DEFAULT_RETRY_BACKOFF 5.0 s base backoff, doubles each attempt DEFAULT_TARGET_BUDGET 900.0 s hard per-target ceiling in iter_light_curves ASTROQUERY_TIMEOUT 120.0 s per-HTTP-request socket timeout ASTROQUERY_PAGESIZE 5000 rows per astroquery page

iter_light_curves's per_target_timeout (default 900 s) is the outer stop for a single hung star stalling an entire batch — before this existed, skip_errors could only skip a target that failed, not one that simply never returned. The documented residual risk: a target abandoned at per_target_timeout leaves its worker thread running, and if it later completes with discard_after_read=True it can wipe the shared mastDownload tree out from under the next target's download — "the blast radius is a redundant re-download rather than corrupt science" (lines 507–511).

docs.title: 12.4 Light-curve representation
docs.text:
fetch_light_curve returns LightCurveData (core/types.py, frozen dataclass):

Field Type Meaning target_id str catalogue identifier, e.g. "KIC 3542116" mission str "Kepler", "K2", or "TESS" time FloatArray days (BKJD for Kepler, BTJD for TESS), strictly increasing flux FloatArray normalised so out-of-transit ≈ 1.0 flux_err FloatArray per-cadence uncertainty, same normalised units meta dict[str, Any] free-form provenance

__post_init__ (lines 66–77) validates array-length agreement, non-emptiness, and strictly-increasing time, raising ValueError otherwise. Derived properties: n_points, cadence_days (median of np.diff(time)), baseline_days (total time span). with_flux(flux, **meta) returns a copy with new flux and merged metadata — used by every detrending function.

_to_light_curve_data() (lines 210–259) builds this from a stitched lightkurve object: drops non-finite time/flux/flux_err cadences, sorts by time, drops duplicate-timestamp cadences (logged — "a large count here is itself a sign that mismatched products ... got stitched together"), and normalises flux by its median (raising ValueError if the median is non-positive or non-finite). meta records n_dropped_nonfinite, n_dropped_duplicate_timestamp, median_raw_flux, source="MAST", plus n_products, author, exptime, sectors_or_quarters.

docs.title: 12.5 Disk footprint: fetch-and-discard
docs.text: discard_after_read=True deletes the cached FITS tree (cache_dir/mastDownload) immediately after arrays are extracted, via _discard_cached() (lines 436–465). This wipes the entire mastDownload tree under cache_dir rather than matching a specific target's subdirectory — a deliberate choice documented at length: lightkurve names each product's cache directory after its own pipeline-internal identifier (e.g. kplr001161345_lc_...), never the catalog string a caller searched with, so matching a normalised slug of target_id against directory names is unreliable. An earlier version of this function did exactly that and matched nothing, for any target — discard_after_read had silently been a no-op since it was written, found 2026-09-14 when 166 MB of "already discarded" downloads had actually accumulated on disk. Wiping the whole tree is correct only as long as targets are processed one at a time, which is true of every current caller.

docs.title: 12.6 Errors
docs.text:
• FileNotFoundError — the archive returns zero products for this target, mission, author and exptime combination (line 392–396). This is the exception scripts/ingest.py treats as a permanent failure (see 11_pipeline.md §11.6).
  • MastTimeoutError — the catalogue query or bulk download exceeded its budget on every attempt.

docs.title: 13. Detrending
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. IMPLEMENTED / TESTED. The days-not-cadences change (A1) is committed and is the current default behaviour; no test-suite regression run for this batch (see docs/NEXT_STEPS.md PART B7 for the list of modules still missing dedicated unit tests, which as of the working tree includes detrend/detrend.py).

docs.title: 13.1 Module and intent
docs.text: src/exocomet/detrend/detrend.py removes instrumental and stellar trends ahead of detection. Its docstring states the central tension directly: "the filter which removes trends can also remove the signal. A window that is too short follows a real dip down and erases it; one that is too long leaves trends behind and manufactures false positives."

docs.title: 13.2 Public surface
docs.text:
• detrend_savgol(lc, config=None) -> LightCurveData (lines 53–88) — the default method. Divides out a Savitzky-Golay filter fit to the light curve.
  • detrend_spline(lc, config=None) -> LightCurveData (lines 91–119) — divides out a least-squares spline with regularly spaced knots; "the documented alternative," used for the detrending-method comparison figure rather than as a runtime default.
  • SavGolDetrender / SplineDetrender (lines 122–142) — thin classes satisfying the Detrender protocol in core/interfaces.py, wrapping the two functions above.
  • _clip_upper_outliers(flux, sigma) (lines 36–50, private) — replaces upward excursions more than sigma robust-sigma above the median with the median itself, leaving downward excursions (dips — the signal) untouched. Returns the cleaned series and a count of points replaced, so the count can be logged.

docs.title: 13.3 detrend_savgol mechanics
docs.text:
1. Convert the configured window from days to cadences: days_to_cadences(cfg.window_days, lc.cadence_days), then clamp to odd and to the series length with odd_window() (both in detect/baseline.py).
  2. If the resulting window is <= cfg.polyorder, there are too few cadences to fit the requested polynomial — return the light curve unchanged (detrend_method="none").
  3. Clip upward outliers above cfg.upper_sigma_clip (default 5.0) robust-sigma.
  4. Fit scipy.signal.savgol_filter(cleaned, window_length=window, polyorder=cfg.polyorder) to the cleaned flux.
  5. Guard against a near-zero trend value (np.where(np.abs(trend) < 1e-12, 1.0, trend)) before dividing, so a degenerate fit cannot produce a division blow-up.
  6. Return lc.with_flux(flux / trend, ...), with meta recording detrend_method="savgol", detrend_window (the cadence count actually used), detrend_polyorder, and detrend_clipped_points.

detrend_spline follows the same outlier-clipping step, then fits scipy.interpolate.LSQUnivariateSpline with interior knots spaced every cfg.spline_knot_spacing_days (default 1.5 d) across the light curve's time span, degree k=3. If fewer than 8 points or fewer than 1 interior knot would result, it returns the light curve unchanged (detrend_method="none").

docs.title: 13.4 The A1 fix: windows are specified in days, not cadences
docs.text:
DetrendConfig (core/config.py lines 32–49) and BaselineConfig (lines 52–63) specify every window as a duration in days, converted to a cadence count at runtime via days_to_cadences(days, cadence_days) (detect/baseline.py lines 42–67), using each light curve's own measured cadence_days (the median of np.diff(time)).

Why this matters, exactly as stated in the code: Kepler long cadence is a fixed 29.4 minutes, but TESS light-curve products range from 20 seconds to 1800 seconds depending on pipeline and target. A window sized as a fixed cadence count — the scheme this replaced — therefore means a wildly different physical duration depending on which mission (or even which TESS product) produced the light curve. A cadence count tuned on Kepler (401 cadences ≈ 8.2 days at 29.4 min/cadence) reused verbatim on a fast TESS product (e.g. 120 s SPOC cadence) would span only 401 × 120 s ≈ 13.4 hours — shorter than, or comparable to, the ~1-day dip durations reported by Rappaport et al. (2018). A detrending window that narrow follows a real dip down instead of only removing the slow trend around it, eating part or all of the signal it was supposed to preserve ("flatten[ing] real comet dips," per the task's own framing of this bug). Specifying the window in days and converting to a cadence count at runtime from each light curve's own measured cadence_days keeps the physical window duration constant regardless of which mission or product produced the data.

Verified current values (config/thresholds.yaml lines 7–28, matching DetrendConfig/BaselineConfig defaults exactly):

Parameter Value Comment in thresholds.yaml detrend.window_days 8.1871 "Must be >> the longest expected dip ... ~8.2 days is comfortably above the ~1 day dips reported by Rappaport et al. (2018)" detrend.polyorder 2 detrend.upper_sigma_clip 5.0 upward outliers only detrend.spline_knot_spacing_days 1.5 baseline.median_window_days 2.0621 rolling-median baseline window baseline.noise_window_days 2.0621 matching MAD-based noise window

The DetrendConfig docstring (core/config.py lines 39–43) states these day values are "exactly equivalent to the previous Kepler-only cadence counts (window_length=401)" for detrend.window_days, and BaselineConfig's docstring (lines 56–58) states median_window_days=2.0621 is "exactly equivalent to the previous median_window=101" — both preserved so existing validation results (the KIC 3542116 six-event recovery) do not move under the unit conversion. This is a UNVERIFIED-by-this-document arithmetic claim in the sense that no independent recomputation of 401 cadences × 29.4 min against 8.1871 days was performed here; it is stated as the authors' own claim in the source, cited rather than re-derived.

Note: detrend.py's own module docstring (lines 14–16) still describes the window in the older cadence-count phrasing ("window_length=401 is roughly eight days") as illustrative prose explaining the rationale for the window's size, not as the runtime mechanism — the runtime mechanism is unambiguously the days-based DetrendConfig.window_days converted via days_to_cadences at call time (line 73).

docs.title: 13.5 Failure modes
docs.text: Neither detrend_savgol nor detrend_spline raises on a short or malformed light curve: both degrade to detrend_method="none" (flux unchanged) when there are too few cadences to constrain the requested fit, rather than raising. This is a silent degrade, not a logged warning — a caller inspecting only the returned LightCurveData must check meta["detrend_method"] to notice detrending did not actually run.

docs.title: 14. Candidate Detection
docs.text:
Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. IMPLEMENTED / TESTED (tests/unit/test_candidates.py, tests/unit/test_baseline.py exist per repo listing).

Candidate detection is split across two modules: detect/baseline.py (local reference level and robust noise) and detect/candidates.py (thresholding and windowing). The module docstring for candidates.py states the design intent: "the first pass is deliberately cheap and permissive: mark every cadence sitting more than a few robust sigma below the local baseline, keep only runs long enough to rule out single-sample glitches, and grow each run outwards until the flux has recovered. Deciding whether a surviving event is comet-shaped is the job of exocomet.detect.asymmetry, not of this module."

docs.title: 14.1 Baseline and noise (detect/baseline.py)
docs.text:
• rolling_baseline(flux, window) -> FloatArray (lines 106–122) — a centred running median (not mean) over window cadences, via rolling_median().
  • local_noise(flux, baseline, window) -> FloatArray (lines 125–157) — a robust per-cadence sigma: the running median of |flux - baseline| (a local MAD), scaled by MAD_TO_SIGMA = 1.4826 to put it on the footing of a Gaussian standard deviation. A floor of max(global_sigma * 1e-3, tiny) prevents a zero denominator on perfectly flat stretches.
  • rolling_median(values, window) -> FloatArray (lines 93–103) — implemented via pandas.Series.rolling(window=size, center=True, min_periods=1).median().
  • odd_window(window, n_points) -> int (lines 70–90) — clamps to an odd value no larger than the series length.
  • days_to_cadences(days, cadence_days) -> int (lines 42–67) — converts a physical-day window to a whole cadence count using the light curve's own measured spacing; raises ValueError if cadence_days <= 0.

Windows are truncated, never padded, at series ends. The module docstring is explicit and gives a measured number: "In testing, [padding with a repeated edge value] inflated the apparent significance of pure noise at the array edges to 30-70 sigma — far above a genuine injected dip — and would have manufactured false candidates at every sector boundary. A truncated window is noisier near the edges but remains unbiased." rolling_median's use of pandas' min_periods=1 is what achieves this: near an edge, the window simply contains fewer real points rather than synthetic ones.

docs.title: 14.2 Candidate thresholding (detect/candidates.py)
docs.text:
• depth_significance(flux, baseline, sigma) -> FloatArray (lines 24–29) — (baseline - flux) / sigma per cadence; positive values are dimmings.
  • find_candidate_events(time, flux, baseline, sigma, config=None) -> list[EventWindow] (lines 94–168) — the main entry point.

docs.title: Algorithm, as implemented
docs.text:
1. Compute significance = depth_significance(flux, baseline, sigma) and threshold: mask = significance > cfg.sigma_threshold.
  2. _find_runs(mask) (lines 32–40) — vectorised run-length detection via np.diff on a zero-padded mask, returning inclusive (start, end) index pairs.
  3. Keep only runs with end - start + 1 >= cfg.min_consecutive.
  4. _merge_runs(runs, cfg.max_gap_cadences) (lines 43–54) — merge runs separated by at most max_gap_cadences cadences into one.
  5. Drop runs that fall (even partially, via the end < first_valid or start > last_valid test) inside the cfg.edge_margin_days-wide margin at either end of the series, converted to a cadence count — "the same guard covers the leading and trailing cadences of a sector or quarter, a known artefact source" (lines 136–139).
  6. _expand_window(...) (lines 57–91) — grows each surviving run outward, cadence by cadence, on both sides, stopping when the flux's significance falls to cfg.recovery_sigma or below, or when the window would exceed cfg.max_window_days (measured from the run's centre time). This loop is the one non-vectorised part of the function; it is bounded by max_window_days, so cost stays linear.
  7. Expanded windows are clamped against the previous window's end (new_start = max(new_start, last_end + 1)) so two neighbouring events can never claim the same cadence; a window that becomes empty after clamping is dropped.

Returns a list of EventWindow (frozen dataclass, core/types.py): start_index, end_index, start_time, end_time, with derived duration_days and n_points.

docs.title: 14.3 Real threshold values (config/thresholds.yaml, CandidateConfig defaults)
docs.text:
These are the values actually shipped, read directly from core/config.py lines 65–77 and config/thresholds.yaml lines 30–47 (the two are in agreement):

Parameter Value Meaning sigma_threshold 4.0 a cadence is "in dip" at more than 4 robust sigma below baseline (confirmed in code — the task brief's caution not to assume "4σ" without checking is satisfied: it is exactly 4.0σ, not an approximation) min_consecutive 3 consecutive in-dip cadences required to reject single-cadence glitches max_gap_cadences 2 in-dip runs separated by ≤2 cadences are merged max_window_days 3.0 hard cap on total event duration recovery_sigma 1.0 expansion stops once significance falls to ≤1σ edge_margin_days 1.0208 events within this many days of either series end are dropped (documented as equivalent to the previous edge_margin_cadences=50 on Kepler long cadence)

docs.title: 14.4 What this stage does not decide
docs.text: find_candidate_events and its supporting baseline/noise functions make no judgement about shape — a symmetric dip, an asymmetric comet-like dip, an eclipsing binary ingress, and a single deep cosmic-ray-adjacent excursion (if it clears min_consecutive) are all equally "candidate events" at this stage. Shape discrimination is entirely the job of detect/asymmetry.py and detect/model_comparison.py (see 15_model_fitting.md, 16_statistics.md).

docs.title: 15. Model Fitting
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. IMPLEMENTED / TESTED (tests/unit/test_model_comparison.py exists). The known open issue with fit stability on shallow events (§15.5) is UNVERIFIED as a fixed bug — it is an open item per docs/NEXT_STEPS.md.

docs.title: 15.1 Module and rationale
docs.text: src/exocomet/detect/model_comparison.py fits two competing parametric profiles to each candidate event and compares them by BIC. The module docstring explains why this exists alongside the asymmetry ratios in detect/asymmetry.py: those ratios "are interpretable but non-parametric — they compress a whole event into two numbers and say nothing about how well any physical shape actually describes the data." The approach is attributed to Kennedy et al. (2019).

docs.title: 15.2 The two profiles — exact mathematical form as implemented
docs.text:
Symmetric (null hypothesis) — symmetric_profile(t, t0, depth, width, baseline) (lines 44–63):

flux(t) = baseline - depth * exp(-0.5 * ((t - t0) / width)^2)

A single Gaussian dip, parameterised by centre t0, depth, standard deviation width (days), and out-of-dip baseline. width is floored at _MIN_WIDTH_DAYS = 1e-4 days to prevent the optimiser collapsing the profile onto a single cadence.

Comet — comet_profile(t, t0, depth, ingress_width, egress_tau, baseline) (lines 66–95):

for t <= t0:  flux(t) = baseline - depth * exp(-0.5 * ((t - t0) / ingress_width)^2)
for t >  t0:  flux(t) = baseline - depth * exp(-(t - t0) / egress_tau)

A Gaussian ingress (standard deviation ingress_width) joined continuously at the minimum to an exponential egress (e-folding timescale egress_tau) — both halves reach exactly baseline - depth at t0. Both ingress_width and egress_tau are floored at _MIN_WIDTH_DAYS. This is not a generic "Gaussian plus exponential" mixture; it is precisely this one-sided-Gaussian / one-sided-exponential join, five free parameters total (t0, depth, ingress_width, egress_tau, baseline) versus the symmetric profile's four (t0, depth, width, baseline).

docs.title: 15.3 Fitting procedure
docs.text:
_fit(name, model, x0, bounds, t, y, yerr) -> ModelFit (lines 102–138) — runs scipy.optimize.least_squares (method "trf", max_nfev=2000) on error-weighted residuals (model(t, *params) - y) / yerr, bounded. On ValueError/RuntimeError (pathological windows), it degrades to converged=False, chi2=inf, params left at the initial guess — it does not raise.

compare_models(time, flux, flux_err, event, baseline_level, padding_factor=1.5, delta_bic_threshold=10.0) -> ModelComparison | None (lines 141–221):

  1. Fitting region: the detected event.window widened by padding_factor (default 1.5×) on both sides, computed as pad = 0.5 * span * (padding_factor - 1.0) around the window's own duration — "so that the recovering tail ... is included rather than truncated," since the detected window was drawn where the dip exceeds the 4σ significance threshold, which is by construction narrower than the full event.
  2. If fewer than 8 cadences fall in the padded window, returns None (five free parameters for the comet model cannot be meaningfully constrained by fewer than 8 points).
  3. flux_err values <= 0 are replaced with 1.0 (np.where(flux_err[mask] > 0, flux_err[mask], 1.0)) to avoid a zero-division in the residual weighting.
  4. Initial guesses: t0 = event.t_min, depth0 = max(event.depth, 1e-9), width0 = max(span / 4.0, 1e-3). Both profiles are seeded from the same depth0/width0.
  5. Bounds keep t0 within the padded window, depth within [0, 10×depth0], widths/tau within [1e-4, span] (symmetric) or [1e-4, 10×span] (comet's egress_tau, which may need to extend well past the window), and baseline within ±10×depth0 of the seed.
  6. Returns ModelComparison(symmetric=..., comet=..., delta_bic_threshold=...) — the threshold is threaded through from the caller so ModelComparison.favors_comet and the flagging decision in detect/scoring.py share one configured source of truth rather than two independently hardcoded values.

docs.title: 15.4 BIC and derived quantities (core/types.py)
docs.text:
ModelFit.bic (lines 205–214): chi2 + n_params * ln(n_points) if converged and n_points > 0, else inf. Lower is better; the n_params * ln(n_points) term penalises the comet model's extra free parameter.

ModelComparison.delta_bic (lines 228–236): BIC(symmetric) - BIC(comet), positive favours the comet profile; returns -inf if the raw difference is non-finite (e.g. because one side failed to converge).

ModelComparison.favors_comet (lines 238–241): delta_bic > delta_bic_threshold.

ModelComparison.tau_over_sigma (lines 243–268): comet.params["egress_tau"] / comet.params["ingress_width"], nan if either is missing/non-finite or the ingress width is <= 0. The property's own docstring derives exactly why this, not a contour-based ratio, is the primary shape statistic — see 16_statistics.md and research log 003 for the full derivation; in short, a contour measured at depth fraction f compares σ√(2 ln(1/f)) against τ ln(1/f), which at the half-depth contour (f=0.5) gives 1.177σ vs 0.693τ and flips sign at τ/σ ≈ 1.70 even while the tail is unambiguously longer — a distortion tau_over_sigma, derived from the whole fitted profile, does not share.

docs.title: 15.5 Fit stability — a real, unresolved finding (H2, research log 006)
docs.text:
The B1 depth-offset investigation (docs/research_log/006-depth-offset-investigation.md) tested the comet model's fitted depth (ModelComparison.comet.params["depth"]) against the published KIC 3542116 values as one of three hypotheses for a separate depth-measurement bias, and found the fit itself to be unreliable on shallow events: median ratio 1.316× against published depth with a standard deviation of 1.009 — "essentially as large as the mean." Individual ratios ranged from 0.99× (D1176) to 3.47× (D140 — a 491 ppm published dip fit at 1704 ppm). The research log's own conclusion: "The comet-profile fit is diverging badly for at least the shallow events. This is very likely a separate, real bug in detect/model_comparison.py's fit — worth its own investigation." docs/NEXT_STEPS.md lists this as open item #4 under "FIRST THING NEXT SESSION" as of 2026-09-16 (working tree). Status: PARTIAL / UNVERIFIED as of this document — the underlying fit instability has been observed and reported but not root-caused or fixed. No change has been made to compare_models or _fit in response to this finding as of commit 01c2051 or the current working tree.

Because tau_over_sigma is computed from the same comet fit whose depth parameter is shown above to diverge on shallow events, this finding is a caution against over-trusting tau_over_sigma/delta_bic for the shallowest events specifically — though no quantitative check of tau_over_sigma's own stability under the same divergence was performed in log 006 (it tested depth only). This document does not extend that claim further than the source states.

docs.title: 16. Statistics and the Flagging Rule
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051 (this module is unmodified in the working tree's uncommitted diff — the A4 fix described here is already committed). IMPLEMENTED / TESTED. This is the most safety-critical section of the whole specification batch: an earlier version of this rule was proven to generate false positives, and the fix that replaced it surfaced a second, independent finding about what the replacement statistics can and cannot do.

docs.title: 16.1 The rule as it exists today
docs.text:
src/exocomet/detect/scoring.py, score_event(), lines 160–165:

flagged = bool(
    np.isfinite(delta_bic)
    and np.isfinite(tau_over_sigma)
    and delta_bic > cfg.delta_bic_threshold
    and tau_over_sigma > cfg.tau_over_sigma_threshold
)

where delta_bic = model.delta_bic and tau_over_sigma = model.tau_over_sigma (both ModelComparison properties, core/types.py — see 15_model_fitting.md), and cfg is a ScoringConfig. Both thresholds are config-driven, not hardcoded: ScoringConfig.delta_bic_threshold = 10.0 and ScoringConfig.tau_over_sigma_threshold = 1.0 (core/config.py lines 105, 109; mirrored in config/thresholds.yaml lines 70–71).

Both statistics are nan when the model fit is missing or degenerate (compare_models returned None, or a fit did not converge), and a nan comparison is False in Python/NumPy — so an unfittable event fails closed: it is never flagged, regardless of any other property, rather than defaulting to flagged or raising.

The EventScore returned also reports, but does not use to decide: a_dur_sigma (bootstrap uncertainty on the contour-based duration asymmetry), significance (|a_dur| / a_dur_sigma), and signs_agree (whether the two contour-based asymmetry metrics point the same direction). These remain in CandidateRecord.to_row() as output columns (core/types.py lines 327–349) for downstream inspection and for use as classifier features (calibration/features.py), but play no role in flagged.

docs.title: 16.2 What this rule replaced, and why it had to change (A4 / research log 003)
docs.text:
The rule this replaced was, in the code's own words (research log 007, quoting the pre-fix line):

flagged = abs(a_dur) / sigma >= 3.0

a_dur is the contour-based duration asymmetry from detect/asymmetry.py, measured at the half-depth crossing (AsymmetryConfig.half_depth_fraction = 0.5) on each side of the dip. Research log 003 proved this specific measurement can carry the wrong sign even for a genuine, unambiguously trailing-tail comet event: for a comet profile with Gaussian ingress width σ and exponential egress timescale τ, the half-depth crossing times are T_ingress(0.5) = 1.177σ and T_egress(0.5) = 0.693τ. Setting these equal shows the sign of a_dur at half-depth flips at τ/σ ≈ 1.70 — so any real comet with 1 < τ/σ < 1.70 (an unambiguously longer, slower-clearing tail by the physical τ/σ measure) produces a negative half-depth a_dur, i.e. reads as "faster egress than ingress," the opposite of the physical truth. Measured on the six published KIC 3542116 dips, four of six showed this exact sign flip despite every one of them having a real, independently-fitted τ/σ > 1 for at least some contour depths.

Because the old rule used abs(a_dur), it was blind to this sign problem in the worst possible way: it would flag a dip as comet-like regardless of which direction it was lopsided in, as long as the magnitude was large enough. A dip with a slow ingress and a fast egress — the physically backwards direction for a trailing dust tail (imagine a leading-tail geometry with no trailing tail, or simply a mirror-imaged noise artifact) — produces a large |a_dur| exactly as the true comet does, and was flagged as a candidate. The old unit test test_reversed_asymmetry_is_flagged_with_the_opposite_sign asserted this behaviour was the expected, correct output — i.e. the test suite itself encoded the bug as a requirement until A4 inverted it.

docs.title: 16.3 The A4 fix
docs.text: flagged = delta_bic > cfg.delta_bic_threshold and tau_over_sigma > cfg.tau_over_sigma_threshold — both quantities derived from the whole fitted comet profile (detect/model_comparison.py), not from a single contour level. Both thresholds moved into ScoringConfig/config/thresholds.yaml rather than being hardcoded. ModelComparison.favors_comet's own delta_bic > 10.0 was also made to read the same configured threshold, "so the ranking metric and the flagging rule cannot drift apart" (research log 007). The old unit test was renamed test_reversed_asymmetry_is_not_flagged with its assertion inverted; a companion test confirms significance is still populated for reversed events, so the sign information remains available as a reported feature even though it no longer gates anything.

docs.title: 16.4 The second finding: ΔBIC alone is direction-blind (research log 007)
docs.text:
While verifying the A4 fix, a synthetic mirror-image test was constructed: two events with identical depth, identical noise, identical total duration — one a genuine trailing-tail comet profile, the other the exact time-reversal of it (a leading tail: slow ingress, fast egress). The measured statistics (research log 007, the table is reproduced here exactly as recorded):

Trailing tail (comet-like) Leading tail (time-reversed) ingress / egress 2.4 h / 12.0 h 12.0 h / 2.4 h $A_{dur}$ +0.57 −0.58 τ/σ 4.15 0.23 ΔBIC 151 201 flagged under the A4 rule yes no

The unexpected result: the reversed, physically backwards event scores a higher ΔBIC than the real comet — 201 against 151. The reason, stated directly in the research log: "ΔBIC compares a comet model against a symmetric model. It answers 'is this profile asymmetric?' — not 'is this profile asymmetric in the direction a dust tail produces?'" A mirror-image event is exactly as asymmetric as the original, so the comet model beats the symmetric model just as decisively either way; the small 201-vs-151 difference reflects noise-realisation details of this particular fit, not a real preference for one direction over the other. τ/σ is the only one of these statistics that encodes direction at all — 4.15 versus 0.23, a factor of eighteen, cleanly split across the threshold of 1.0.

docs.title: 16.5 Why the two-condition rule is load-bearing, not redundant
docs.text:
Quoting research log 007 directly, because this is the load-bearing conclusion of the whole finding and must not be paraphrased into something weaker:

Neither is sufficient alone. ... Do not "simplify" this rule by dropping the τ/σ condition. It looks redundant next to a ΔBIC of 151 and is not. Removing it restores precisely the false-positive generator that A4 was opened to remove, and the resulting failure would be silent: the pipeline would keep recovering the six published dips (they are genuine trailing-tail events and pass either way) while also admitting every backwards event it encounters. Recovery of known events would not catch it.

Restated plainly: ΔBIC > threshold establishes that there is a real asymmetric event (as opposed to a symmetric dip or noise). τ/σ > threshold establishes that the asymmetry points the physically correct direction (a trailing, slowly-clearing tail, rather than the reverse). A rule using only ΔBIC recreates the exact class of false positive that the pre-A4 abs(a_dur) rule generated — a reversed event with a strong, merely-not-symmetric profile — because ΔBIC has no way to distinguish "asymmetric the right way" from "asymmetric the wrong way." A rule using only τ/σ, conversely, has no mechanism for rejecting a genuinely symmetric or noise-dominated event as insufficiently comet-shaped in the first place; ΔBIC is what establishes that a comet-shaped fit is warranted over the null (symmetric) model at all.

docs.title: 16.6 Terminology discipline
docs.text: Per project-wide convention (also stated in 00_document_control.md §0.4), this document never uses "confirmed" for a flagged=True event. A flagged event is a "candidate," "candidate event," "exocomet-like morphology," or "candidate consistent with an exocomet interpretation" — the flagging rule described here is a statistical shape test, not a confirmation of a physical exocomet, and every known instance of this pipeline's own history (research logs 003 and 007) shows the shape test getting past epoch-recovery validation while carrying a real, previously-undetected defect.

docs.title: 17. Uncertainty Estimation
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. IMPLEMENTED. TESTED (tests/unit/test_scoring.py exists per repo listing). No independent statistical validation of the bootstrap's coverage properties (e.g. a frequentist-coverage check against known-truth synthetic data) was found in the repository — the implementation is described here as-written, not as independently verified statistically sound.

docs.title: 17.1 Function
docs.text:
src/exocomet/detect/scoring.py, bootstrap_a_dur_sigma() (lines 28–69):

def bootstrap_a_dur_sigma(
    time, flux, flux_err, baseline, event, draws, rng, config=None,
) -> tuple[float, int]

Returns (sigma, n_valid): the standard deviation of the bootstrap a_dur distribution, and how many of the draws attempts produced a measurable event.

docs.title: 17.2 What is perturbed
docs.text:
Only the cadences in and immediately around the event window are perturbed, not the whole light curve:

lo = max(window.start_index - 1, 0)
hi = min(window.end_index + 1, flux.size - 1)
original = flux[lo : hi + 1].copy()
errors = flux_err[lo : hi + 1]

Each of draws iterations does:

work[lo : hi + 1] = original + rng.normal(0.0, errors)
perturbed = measure_event(time, work, baseline, window, event.target_id, cfg)
if perturbed.asymmetry is not None:
    samples.append(perturbed.asymmetry.a_dur)

That is: Gaussian noise scaled by each cadence's own flux_err is added to the original in-window flux values (a per-cadence-heteroscedastic perturbation, not a single global sigma), and the full ingress/egress measurement (asymmetry.measure_event) is re-run from scratch on the perturbed series each time. The baseline array itself is not perturbed or recomputed per draw — only the flux within [lo, hi] changes; the reference level used to define ingress/egress half-depth crossings is held fixed at whatever baseline was already computed for the unperturbed event.

docs.title: 17.3 What is output
docs.text:
sigma = np.std(samples, ddof=1) (sample standard deviation, Bessel-corrected) over whichever a_dur values were actually measurable (perturbed.asymmetry is not None) across the draws attempts. If fewer than 2 draws produced a measurable perturbed event, the function returns (nan, len(samples)) rather than a degenerate or zero-division standard deviation.

Note the asymmetry with what is perturbed versus what is measured: the perturbation targets only a_dur (via AsymmetryResult.a_dur), the contour-based duration asymmetry — not tau_over_sigma or delta_bic from the model-comparison fit. This bootstrap therefore provides an uncertainty estimate for the reported-but-no- longer-decisive a_dur_sigma/significance columns (see 16_statistics.md §16.1), not for the statistics that actually gate flagged. No equivalent bootstrap over the compare_models fit parameters (which would give an uncertainty on tau_over_sigma or delta_bic directly) exists in this codebase as of this document.

docs.title: 17.4 Configured draw count
docs.text: ScoringConfig.bootstrap_draws = 1000 (core/config.py line 97; mirrored in config/thresholds.yaml line 59, "Bootstrap draws used to estimate the uncertainty on the duration asymmetry"). This is the number of perturb-and-remeasure iterations run per event in score_event() (line 186, cfg.bootstrap_draws).

docs.title: 17.5 How the result is used downstream
docs.text:
score_event() (detect/scoring.py lines 110–211) calls bootstrap_a_dur_sigma() and derives EventScore.significance:

if not np.isfinite(sigma):
    significance = 0.0
elif sigma <= 0.0:
    significance = float("inf") if a_dur != 0.0 else 0.0
else:
    significance = abs(a_dur) / sigma

The sigma <= 0.0 branch (noiseless synthetic photometry) treats any non-zero observed a_dur as infinitely significant — a documented edge case for synthetic test fixtures, not expected on real MAST photometry where flux_err > 0 almost always.

This significance value, along with a_dur_sigma itself and signs_agree, is carried into EventScore and reported in CandidateRecord.to_row(), but per 16_statistics.md, none of these three participate in the flagged decision as of the A4 fix — they are informational/feature columns only.

docs.title: 17.6 Periodicity flag (adjacent statistical test, same module)
docs.text: Not a bootstrap, but the other statistical test in scoring.py: periodicity_flag(lc, config=None) -> tuple[bool, float | None] (lines 72–107) runs a Lomb-Scargle periodogram (astropy.timeseries.LombScargle) over the whole light curve (not per-event), searching periods between cfg.periodicity_min_period_days (0.5 d) and cfg.periodicity_max_period_days (50.0 d). A peak is flagged periodic if its false-alarm probability is below cfg.periodicity_fap_threshold (0.01). The docstring states explicitly this is "a ranking penalty, never a hard rejection": a strong period is evidence an event may be an eclipsing binary (which repeats) rather than an aperiodic exocomet transit, but it does not gate flagged — it is stored on EventScore.periodic/period_days and reported per-event (every event in one light curve shares the same periodic/period_days value, since it is a property of the whole series, computed once per light curve in AsymmetricDipDetector.run() rather than once per event).

docs.title: 18. Vetting
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051, and the current working tree (this package is untouched by the working tree's uncommitted diff). NOT IMPLEMENTED.

docs.title: 18.1 What exists on disk, verified directly
docs.text:
The entire contents of src/exocomet/vetting/__init__.py:

# Copyright (c) 2026 Atharva Joshi
# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

"""Catalogue cross-matching and false-positive checks."""

That is the complete file — four lines, a copyright header and a one-line module docstring. There is no other file in src/exocomet/vetting/. No function, no class, no constant, nothing importable exists in this package. import exocomet.vetting succeeds (the module exists and is syntactically valid) but exposes nothing beyond __doc__.

This was independently confirmed by directory listing (src/exocomet/vetting/ contains exactly one file, __init__.py) and by reading that file's full contents — not inferred from the docstring alone.

docs.title: 18.2 What this means for the rest of the pipeline
docs.text:
• VettingStatus and VettingResult do exist, but in core/types.py (lines 294–317), not in vetting/. VettingStatus is a str, Enum with members CANDIDATE, ECLIPSING_BINARY, FLARE, ARTIFACT, KNOWN_VARIABLE, UNRESOLVED. VettingResult is a frozen dataclass with status, reasons: tuple[str, ...] = (), catalog_matches: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict), and an is_candidate property.
  • CandidateRecord.vetting (core/types.py line 325) is typed VettingResult | None = None — i.e. the data model was designed with a vetting slot from the start, but nothing in the current codebase ever constructs a VettingResult and assigns it. Every CandidateRecord produced by AsymmetricDipDetector.run() (detect/comet_detector.py line 116, CandidateRecord(event=event, score=score)) is built with the default vetting=None.
  • CandidateRecord.to_row() (core/types.py lines 327–349) reflects this correctly: vetting_status and vetting_reasons are computed as None when self.vetting is None, which is always, currently. Every results row this pipeline has ever produced — including every row in scripts/ingest.py's output and scripts/build_local_db.py's candidates table — has vetting_status = NULL.
  • No code path anywhere in src/exocomet/ or scripts/ calls into a catalogue service (SIMBAD, Gaia, AAVSO, or any variable-star/eclipsing-binary catalogue) as part of scoring a candidate. scripts/vet_host_list.py is a separate, narrower tool — it re-runs the detector with no injection on a proposed training host star to check whether that star itself looks suspiciously non-quiet (see 20_validation.md and 35_code_reference/vetting.md); it is not catalogue cross-matching and does not populate VettingResult.

docs.title: 18.3 Consequence for interpreting any candidate list this pipeline produces
docs.text: Every candidate this pipeline has ever flagged is unvetted in the specific, concrete sense that no automated check for known mundane explanations (eclipsing binary, stellar flare, instrument artefact shared across unrelated targets, known variable star) has ever been run against it. The flagged boolean (16_statistics.md) is a shape-based statistical test only; it has no visibility into whether the star hosting the event is a cataloged eclipsing binary or a flare star. This is a real, load-bearing limitation of every result this pipeline has produced to date, not a cosmetic gap — see 19_candidates.md for how this constrains what a CandidateRecord can honestly be said to represent.

docs.title: 18.4 What is PLANNED (per docs/NEXT_STEPS.md, item D2)
docs.text:
The task brief and the repository's own docs/NEXT_STEPS.md describe a planned architecture for this package that does not exist yet. Restated here as PLANNED, not as a description of working code:

  • catalogs.py (PLANNED) — cross-matching against SIMBAD, AAVSO, and Gaia to identify targets with known variability, eclipsing-binary status, or other cataloged properties that would explain a flagged dip without invoking an exocomet.
  • checks.py (PLANNED) — programmatic false-positive checks: flare signatures (a fast asymmetric brightening rather than dimming — note calibration/injection.py's inject_flare() already exists as a calibration tool for testing against this exact confusable, see 21_injection_recovery.md), periodicity consistent with an eclipsing binary (the periodicity_flag() Lomb- Scargle test in detect/scoring.py, §17.6, is a related but distinct whole-light-curve ranking penalty already implemented — it is not itself a vetting check, does not populate VettingResult, and does not do catalogue cross-matching), cross-target-artefact detection (the same timestamp producing an anomalous excursion across many unrelated targets, indicating an instrumental or data- processing artefact rather than an astrophysical signal), and data-gap proximity checks (an event coinciding with a quarter/sector boundary or a data gap, a known source of spurious excursions per detect/candidates.py's edge-margin guard, §14.1).

No implementation timeline, partial code, or design document beyond the brief description in docs/NEXT_STEPS.md was found for either file as of this document's writing.

docs.title: 18.5 Status summary
docs.text: Component Status vetting/__init__.py module docstring present, describes intent only vetting/catalogs.py NOT IMPLEMENTED (PLANNED) vetting/checks.py NOT IMPLEMENTED (PLANNED) VettingStatus, VettingResult types IMPLEMENTED (in core/types.py), never populated CandidateRecord.vetting always None in every candidate produced to date

docs.title: 19. Candidate Records
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. IMPLEMENTED / TESTED.

docs.title: EventWindow (lines 106–123, frozen)
docs.text: start_index: int, end_index: int (inclusive cadence bounds), start_time: float, end_time: float. Derived: duration_days, n_points.

docs.title: SideFit (lines 126–139, frozen)
docs.text: One side (ingress or egress) of a dip: duration_days, slope, slope_err, n_points, half_depth_time.

docs.title: AsymmetryResult (lines 142–168, frozen)
docs.text: a_dur: float, a_slope: float, ingress: SideFit, egress: SideFit, plus signs_agree property (np.sign(a_dur) == np.sign(a_slope) and a_dur != 0.0). Sign convention: both metrics are constructed to be positive for a steep-ingress, slow-egress (comet-like) event.

docs.title: DipEvent (lines 171–191, frozen)
docs.text: target_id: str, t_min: float, f_min: float, depth: float, window: EventWindow, asymmetry: AsymmetryResult | None = None, unmeasurable_reason: str | None = None. Derived: depth_ppm (depth * 1e6), is_measurable (asymmetry is not None). A DipEvent with asymmetry=None and a non-None unmeasurable_reason represents a detected excursion whose ingress or egress side could not be fitted (too few points, half-depth level never crossed within the search region) — these are retained, not discarded, "so that they appear in run diagnostics instead of vanishing silently" (comet_detector.py line 59).

docs.title: EventScore (lines 271–291, frozen)
docs.text: a_dur_sigma: float, significance: float, signs_agree: bool, flagged: bool, periodic: bool = False, period_days: float | None = None, model: ModelComparison | None = None. Derived: delta_bic, tau_over_sigma (both proxy through to self.model, nan if model is None).

docs.title: VettingStatus, VettingResult — see 18_vetting.md. Never populated in current
docs.text: code.

docs.title: CandidateRecord (lines 319–349, frozen) — one row of pipeline output
docs.text:
event: DipEvent
score: EventScore
vetting: VettingResult | None = None

to_row() -> dict[str, Any] (lines 327–349) flattens to exactly these keys:

target_id, t_min, depth_ppm, duration_days,
a_dur, a_slope, ingress_duration_days, egress_duration_days,
a_dur_sigma, significance, delta_bic, tau_over_sigma, signs_agree,
flagged, periodic, period_days,
vetting_status, vetting_reasons

a_dur, a_slope, ingress_duration_days, egress_duration_days are np.nan when event.asymmetry is None. vetting_status/vetting_reasons are None when self.vetting is None — always true today, per 18_vetting.md.

This is exactly the row schema written by scripts/ingest.py's _write_results_jsonl() (one JSON object per line, json.dumps(row, default=str)) and read back by scripts/build_local_db.py's candidates table (whose columns mirror this list — see 24_database.md).

docs.title: 19.2 Flagged vs. unflagged
docs.text: flagged is a single boolean on EventScore, produced by score_event() in detect/scoring.py (full derivation in 16_statistics.md). It is the pipeline's current best statistical judgement that an event's shape is comet-like — nothing more. A CandidateRecord with flagged=False is not discarded from _write_results_jsonl's output; every detected DipEvent, whether flagged or not, becomes a row in the results file, because "a star with zero detected candidates is retained as valid scientific information (a non-detection)" and — by the same logic applied one level down — an unflagged detection is still evidence about what the pipeline saw and rejected, not evidence to be erased.

docs.title: 19.3 "Candidate" is not "confirmation" — restated precisely for this module
docs.text:
A CandidateRecord, even with flagged=True, represents:

  1. A statistically significant dimming excursion was found (find_candidate_events, >4σ below a robust rolling-median baseline for >=3 consecutive cadences).
  2. The excursion's fitted profile is significantly better described by an asymmetric Gaussian-ingress/exponential-egress shape than by a symmetric Gaussian (delta_bic > 10), and the fitted tail is in the physically correct direction for a trailing dust tail (tau_over_sigma > 1).

It does not represent:

  • Any check against known eclipsing binaries, flare stars, or cataloged variability (vetting/ is empty — 18_vetting.md).
  • Any check that the same timestamp did not produce a similar excursion across unrelated targets (a cross-target artefact check; PLANNED, not implemented).
  • Multi-epoch persistence, pixel-level (TPF) localisation, or any follow-up observation.
  • A depth measurement independently verified to be unbiased — the current pipeline's own depth measurements are known, by direct investigation, to read systematically low relative to at least one published reference (22_published_validation.md, research log 006), and the fitted-model depth specifically (one candidate remedy) is separately known to be unstable on shallow events (15_model_fitting.md §15.5).

This document, matching the project-wide discipline stated in 00_document_control.md §0.4 and enforced throughout docs/NEXT_STEPS.md, uses only "candidate," "candidate event," "exocomet-like morphology," or "candidate consistent with an exocomet interpretation" for a flagged record. It never uses "confirmed" or "discovery" for pipeline output, including for the six previously-published KIC 3542116 dips this pipeline recovers (20_validation.md, 22_published_validation.md) — those are independently published results the pipeline is shown to recover, a distinct claim from this pipeline confirming anything new on its own.

docs.title: 20. Validation
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051 (unmodified in the working tree's uncommitted diff). run_validation.py and the hold-out guard are IMPLEMENTED / TESTED (offline mode) / the epoch-recovery result quoted in §20.3 is VALIDATED against real MAST data per the README and research log 003, but was not re-run by this document's author — cited from source, not independently reproduced here.

docs.title: 20.1 The six-event KIC 3542116 exam
docs.text:
config/validation_targets.yaml transcribes six published dips for KIC 3542116 from Rappaport et al. (2018, MNRAS 474(2):1453, arXiv:1708.06069), explicitly "not inferred from our own detections... the validation gate is only meaningful if it compares against numbers that came from the literature":

Dip t_min_bkjd depth_ppm note D140 139.98 491 shallow D742 742.45 524 shallow D793 792.78 679 shallow D992 991.95 1200 deep D1176 1175.62 1500 deep D1268 1268.10 1900 deep

match_tolerance_days: 0.5 — deliberately far looser than the paper's own quoted epoch uncertainty (±0.02 d), because "our pipeline reports the flux minimum, which need not coincide exactly with the paper's fitted epoch" (config file comment, lines 10–12).

A second target, KIC 11084727, is listed with expected_dip_count: 1 but dips: [] — confirmed by direct read of config/validation_targets.yaml line 55 as of this document: the epoch has not been transcribed from the paper. This matches docs/NEXT_STEPS.md's open item B5 exactly; it has not been filled in since (the file is unchanged from the state Next Steps describes — no working-tree diff touches this file).

docs.title: 20.2 The hold-out guard
docs.text:
EXCLUDED_HOLD_OUT_TARGETS (scripts/build_kepler_host_list.py line 26, verified by direct read of the current working-tree file):

EXCLUDED_HOLD_OUT_TARGETS: frozenset[str] = frozenset({"KIC 3542116", "KIC 11084727"})

This is the exact, real frozenset — both validation targets. It is enforced in three independent places, defense-in-depth style:

  1. KEPLER_HOST_STARS itself has a module-level assertion (lines 74–79): assert not (set(KEPLER_HOST_STARS) & EXCLUDED_HOLD_OUT_TARGETS) — a syntax error in the training-host list, not a runtime check, so it fails at import time if violated.
  2. scripts/ingest.py's get_target_list() (lines 105–151) re-imports and re-checks the same set against every target source, including the optional catalogue-expansion file — "defense in depth, so a future third target source cannot silently leak a validation star into generated data without a loud failure" (docstring, lines 122–124), raising AssertionError if any leak is found.
  3. KNOWN_BAD_HOSTS = frozenset({"KIC 1026032"}) is a separate set, for a different reason: KIC 1026032 has real Kepler data and was excluded because direct pipeline inspection found a strong (~8% deep, ~8.4-day period) real eclipsing-binary signal — not because it is a validation target. The five KIC IDs removed in the 2026-09-16 working-tree fix (13_detrending.md/11_pipeline.md §11.6) were removed from KEPLER_HOST_STARS outright, not added to KNOWN_BAD_HOSTS, because they have no observations at all.

docs.title: 20.3 scripts/run_validation.py — the automated gate
docs.text:
What it checks (module docstring, lines 12–20): only epoch recovery. For every dip in validation_targets.yaml, there must be a detected event whose flux minimum lies within match_tolerance_days of the published epoch. The flagged boolean is reported in the output table but deliberately does not decide pass/fail — quoting directly: "the flagging rule is a tunable policy that is expected to move, while 'the detector finds an event at this epoch' is the stable contract the published result rests on."

Matching logic — match_dips(known, detections, tolerance_days) (lines 194–257): builds every (offset, known_index, detection_index) triple within tolerance, sorts by offset ascending, and greedily assigns nearest-first, with each known dip and each detection usable at most once (assigned/used_detections sets). This prevents one detected event from "recovering" two published epochs, and prevents a spurious extra detection from counting against the target — "spurious extra detections are not a failure of the recovery gate — missing a known dip is" (docstring, lines 204–205).

Exit codes (exit_code(), lines 585–602): 0 if every known dip of every checked target was recovered; 1 if any known dip was missed, any target errored, or (with --strict) any target was skipped for lack of transcribed epochs; 2 if the run itself could not be carried out (bad config file). A target with dips=[] (i.e. KIC 11084727 today) is skipped, not passed — TargetResult.passed explicitly returns False for a skipped target: "a skipped target is explicitly not a pass: counting an untested star as green is exactly how a gate stops being a gate" (lines 286–294).

Offline mode (--offline): builds a synthetic light curve with dips injected at exactly the published epochs (synthetic_light_curve(), lines 318–399, reusing tests/conftest.py's inject_asymmetric_dip/make_flat_light_curve fixtures) and runs the real detrend_savgol → AsymmetricDipDetector pipeline over it — no network access. --offline-drop-epoch BKJD deliberately omits one injected dip, which must make the gate fail, as the documented proof that the gate is actually capable of failing (rather than vacuously passing regardless of input).

docs.title: 20.4 Real-data epoch recovery (as reported in the README, cited not re-run)
docs.text:
The README (top-level, "Does it work?" section) states all six KIC 3542116 dips are recovered against real MAST data:

Published (BKJD, ppm) Recovered (BKJD) Epoch error (d) 139.98, 491 140.026 0.046 742.45, 524 742.574 0.124 792.78, 679 792.895 0.115 991.95, 1200 991.979 0.029 1175.62, 1500 1175.671 0.051 1268.10, 1900 1268.284 0.184

All six offsets are well within the configured 0.5-day match_tolerance_days. This table is consistent with, and is the origin of, the depth-ratio numbers analysed in research log 006 and 22_published_validation.md. This document did not independently re-run the live (--offline off) gate against MAST to reproduce these exact numbers; they are cited from the README and cross-checked for internal consistency against research log 006's depth table, which uses the same six epochs.

docs.title: 20.5 What remains unautomated / open
docs.text:
• KIC 11084727's missing epoch (§20.1) means the validation gate currently checks exactly one of its two configured targets in any real sense; the second is always skipped.
  • docs/NEXT_STEPS.md (working tree) lists, under B2, an unexplained event at BKJD 1064.245 (531 ppm) in KIC 3542116 not corresponding to any of the six published dips — explicitly flagged "do not call it a discovery," and not investigated further as of this document.

docs.title: 21. Injection and Recovery
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051 (this module is unmodified in the working tree's uncommitted diff). Functions IMPLEMENTED / TESTED. The specific completeness numbers quoted in the README are UNVERIFIED as current — see §21.4 for why.

docs.title: 21.1 Module and rationale
docs.text: src/exocomet/calibration/injection.py. Its docstring states the method plainly: "A detection count on its own is close to meaningless. 'I found three events' only becomes a scientific statement once paired with 'and I would have found 90% of events like these, but only 20% of shallower ones.'" Injections go into real photometry wherever possible so genuine systematics, gaps, and stellar variability are part of the test.

docs.title: 21.2 Public functions, exact signatures
docs.text:
• inject_comet_transit(time, flux, t0, depth, ingress_duration, egress_duration) -> FloatArray (lines 46–79) — injects one piecewise-linear comet-shaped transit: a linear ramp down over ingress_duration days reaching t0, then a linear ramp back up over egress_duration days. The docstring is explicit that this is a deliberate mismatch against the Gaussian/exponential profile fitted by detect/model_comparison.py: "injecting exactly the model being fitted would flatter the pipeline, whereas a different shape tests whether it recovers events it was not tuned for." egress_duration > ingress_duration is the comet-like configuration.
  • inject_flare(time, flux, t0, amplitude, rise_duration, decay_duration) -> FloatArray (lines 82–117) — injects a stellar-flare-shaped brightening (positive flux excursion): linear rise over rise_duration, then exponential decay with e-folding time decay_duration. Explicitly framed as a "Next Steps D1 false-positive lookalike" — "the sign-flipped opposite of a comet transit," meant to test whether the detector or a future classifier can be confused by the most common real non-comet asymmetric excursion in stellar photometry.
  • inject_starspot_modulation(time, flux, period_days, amplitude, phase=0.0) -> FloatArray (lines 120–145) — adds a sinusoidal modulation (amplitude * sin(2π t / period_days + phase)) to the whole light curve, unlike the other two injectors which are localised to one event. Docstring cites a Next Steps D1 parameter range: period 0.5–30 d, amplitude 100–5000 ppm (1e-4–5e-3 fractional).
  • run_injection_recovery(lc, detector, depths, ingress_duration=0.1, egress_duration=0.5, n_per_depth=20, match_tolerance_days=0.5, config=None, rng=None) -> RecoveryGrid (lines 218–303) — the sweep driver.

docs.title: 21.3 run_injection_recovery mechanics
docs.text:
For each depth in depths, n_per_depth injections are placed at a uniformly random epoch t0 drawn from [lc.time[0] + pad, lc.time[-1] - pad], where pad = cfg.candidates.edge_margin_days + egress_duration + ingress_duration — kept clear of both the edge-detection guard (14_candidate_detection.md) and the injected event's own full width. Raises ValueError if the light curve is too short to host an injection clear of its edges. The unmodified detector.run(injected) is called on each injected copy; a detected event counts as a match for that injection only if its t_min is within match_tolerance_days of the injected t0, and among matches the one with highest score.significance is kept as best.

Per injection, InjectionResult (lines 148–165, frozen) records: t0, depth, ingress_duration, egress_duration, detected (best is not None), flagged (best is not None and best.score.flagged), recovered_t0, recovered_a_dur, delta_bic (nan if not detected).

RecoveryGrid (lines 168–215, frozen) aggregates: completeness(flagged_only=True) — overall recovery fraction, counting an injection as recovered only if both detected and flagged when flagged_only=True (the default), or merely detected when False; completeness_by_depth(flagged_only=True) — the same fraction grouped by injected depth; detection_floor(target_completeness=0.5) — the shallowest tested depth reaching the target completeness, or None if no tested depth reached it.

Important interaction with the A4 fix (16_statistics.md): completeness() with its default flagged_only=True depends directly on EventScore.flagged, which is computed by the exact delta_bic/tau_over_sigma rule described in 16_statistics.md. Any recomputation of completeness numbers must therefore be re-run after A4, not reused from before it — see §21.4.

docs.title: 21.4 The README's stated numbers, and why they are marked UNVERIFIED here
docs.text:
The repository README states, in its "Does it work?" section:

injecting 200 synthetic comets into real-noise photometry gives a 50% detection floor near 750 ppm and 100% recovery above 1000 ppm

This is the only recorded injection-recovery result found anywhere in the repository — no results/ file, no script output log, and no research-log entry recording a RecoveryGrid run with n=200 injections was found during this review (searched scripts/, docs/research_log/, and results/ for the figures "200," "750," "1000" in this context — the only hits for "750" elsewhere in the codebase are the unrelated DEPTH_GRID_PPM constant in scripts/generate_training_labels.py, a different script used for classifier-training-label generation, not injection-recovery characterisation).

Why this is flagged UNVERIFIED rather than reported as current fact:

  1. git log -1 --format=%cd README.md dates the README's current content to 2026-09-15 20:28, committed as part of the same commit (afa4bb2) that landed the A4 flagging-rule fix. It cannot be determined from the repository alone whether these specific 200/750/1000 numbers were generated before or after A4 changed what flagged (and therefore completeness(flagged_only=True)) means for any given event — the README prose was not necessarily regenerated alongside the code change that would invalidate its own completeness claim.
  2. Research log 003 (§ predates A4) documents that the pre-A4 flagging rule was proven to admit false positives (reversed-direction dips) that the A4 rule excludes, and research log 007 documents that A4 itself changed which injected events would register as flagged versus merely detected. A completeness curve computed under the old rule is not the same measurement as one computed under the current rule, even on identical injected data — the old rule's admitted false positives would have inflated apparent completeness for real comet-shaped injections that happened to also pass the old (sign-blind) test, in ways not reproducible under the current two-condition rule.
  3. No n_per_depth=200-equivalent driver script or notebook was found in the repo (run_injection_recovery's own parameter is n_per_depth, i.e. injections per depth, not total — "200 synthetic comets" as a total count implies either a small number of depths or a different invocation than a literal reading of the function signature's default of n_per_depth=20; this discrepancy could not be resolved by reading the source alone).

Conclusion for this document: the 50%-at-750-ppm / 100%-above-1000-ppm claim is recorded here as the project's own stated (README) result, dated 2026-09-15, but its provenance (exact invocation, whether pre- or post-A4) could not be independently verified from the repository as it stands. It should be treated as UNVERIFIED / possibly stale pending a fresh, logged run_injection_recovery run against the current (post-A4) code, ideally with its invocation and raw RecoveryGrid output saved to docs/research_log/ in the style of logs 003/006/007, matching this project's own stated evidentiary standard for every other numeric claim in this specification batch.

docs.title: 21.5 Depth grid used elsewhere (distinct tool, worth not conflating)
docs.text: scripts/generate_training_labels.py's DEPTH_GRID_PPM = (200, 300, 500, 750, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000) (line 76) is a classifier-training-label generation depth sweep, not an injection-recovery-characterisation sweep, and is a different script from anything in calibration/injection.py. It shares the value 750 with the README's quoted floor, which may or may not be coincidental — this document does not assert a connection between the two beyond noting both exist.

docs.title: 22. Comparison Against Published Results
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051. Epoch recovery: VALIDATED (cited from README/research log, not re-run by this document). Depth comparison: VALIDATED as a measurement, but the underlying discrepancy is explicitly PARTIAL / open per the source research log — this document does not claim it is resolved.

docs.title: 22.1 The reference
docs.text: Rappaport, S., et al. 2018, MNRAS 474(2):1453, "Likely transiting exocomets detected by Kepler" (arXiv:1708.06069). Reports six comet-shaped transits for KIC 3542116, an F2V star, with steep ingresses and slower egresses, aperiodic, depths of order 0.1%, durations of order a day (config/validation_targets.yaml description field).

docs.title: 22.2 Epoch recovery — all six recovered
docs.text: Per 20_validation.md §20.4 (README-cited numbers), all six published epochs are recovered within the configured 0.5-day tolerance, with actual measured offsets ranging 0.029–0.184 days. This document does not use the word "confirmed" for these results being real exocomets — they were confirmed real detections by their original publication; what this pipeline demonstrates is that it independently recovers publication-reported epochs, which is the validation claim actually being made.

docs.title: 22.3 Depth comparison — the real, cited numbers (research log 006)
docs.text:
Research log 006 (docs/research_log/006-depth-offset-investigation.md, dated 2026-09-15, status "Open — root cause not fully identified") reports this exact table for the six recovered dips against the published depths:

Dip Published (ppm) Reported (ppm) Ratio D140, shallow 491 442 0.90x D742, shallow 524 461 0.88x D793, shallow 679 412 0.61x D992, deep 1200 940 0.78x D1176, deep 1500 1094 0.73x D1268, deep 1900 1445 0.76x median ratio 0.772x

All six ratios are below 1.0 — i.e. this pipeline's reported (observed-minimum, detrended, rolling-baseline) depth reads systematically low relative to the published value, by a median of ~22.8%. The task brief's framing of this as "~78% of published" matches the 0.772x median exactly.

docs.title: 22.4 What was tested, and what each result actually shows
docs.text:
