docs.text: Name Value Unit Origin Provenance note target_batch_size 40 stars UNKNOWN No justification in file. shortlist_size 20 candidates UNKNOWN No justification in file.

docs.title: 46.7 runtime section
docs.text: Name Value Unit Origin Provenance note rng_seed 42 — Engineering-choice Comment: "Single seed threaded through every stochastic step, so runs are reproducible." The specific value 42 has no scientific meaning; it is a conventional placeholder seed. max_workers null (→ os.cpu_count() - 1) worker processes Engineering-choice Comment states the resolution rule for null directly.

docs.title: 46.8 Summary
docs.text: Of the 22 parameters enumerated above, 7 have an explicit numeric/physical justification in-file or in a cited reference (window_days, edge_margin_days and median/noise windows via cadence-count continuity plus the Rappaport citation, delta_bic_threshold, tau_over_sigma_threshold, half_depth_fraction, periodicity_fap_threshold), 8 have a stated purpose but no stated derivation for the specific number chosen, and 7 have neither (UNKNOWN). This is a fair characterization of the project's current state: the pipeline is real and validated end-to-end (§43), but a systematic sensitivity/ablation study over these UNKNOWN-origin parameters (Next Steps D4) has not been run.

docs.title: 47. Data Quality Specification
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 47.1 Missing/non-finite data handling — IMPLEMENTED
docs.text:
_to_light_curve_data() in src/exocomet/io/download.py explicitly drops any cadence with a non-finite time, flux, or flux_err value before constructing a LightCurveData:

good = np.isfinite(time) & np.isfinite(flux) & np.isfinite(flux_err)
time, flux, flux_err = time[good], flux[good], flux_err[good]

The count of dropped cadences is recorded in meta["n_dropped_nonfinite"], so it is auditable per light curve rather than silently vanishing. LightCurveData.__post_init__ (core/types.py) additionally enforces strictly increasing time and equal array lengths, raising ValueError on violation — malformed data cannot silently enter the pipeline as a LightCurveData instance.

docs.title: 47.2 Duplicate-timestamp handling — IMPLEMENTED
docs.text: The same function deduplicates cadences with identical or non-increasing timestamps (a real symptom of stitching overlapping quarters/sectors — see 48_experiment_registry.md / Next Steps A2), keeping the first occurrence and logging (not silently dropping) the count as meta["n_dropped_duplicate_timestamp"]. Per the module's own docstring, a large count here is itself diagnostic of mismatched-product stitching, which is why A2 (pinning to a single author/exptime) exists as a fix upstream of this dedup step rather than relying on dedup alone.

docs.title: 47.3 Data-gap handling — PARTIAL / largely NOT IMPLEMENTED
docs.text:
No code in src/exocomet/detrend/detrend.py or src/exocomet/detect/ explicitly detects or special-cases a time gap (e.g. a missing quarter, a safe-mode interruption, a sector boundary). Specifically:

  • detrend_savgol() calls scipy.signal.savgol_filter() on the flux array directly, with a window length expressed in cadence count (converted from window_days via the light curve's own median cadence spacing). savgol_filter operates on array index position, not on the time array — if a real gap exists in the middle of a window, the filter still treats the cadences on either side of the gap as physically adjacent for the purposes of the polynomial fit. This is a known category of systematic error in Savitzky-Golay detrending of gapped time series generally; nothing in this codebase specifically detects or corrects for it.
  • candidates.edge_margin_days (Config §46.3) protects only the two ends of the whole series, not the edges of an internal gap (e.g. a quarter boundary in the middle of a Kepler light curve). The research-log-006 investigation (docs/research_log/006-depth-offset-investigation.md) explicitly names "quarter-to-quarter flux offsets from stitching" as the leading untested suspect for the unexplained portion of the depth-measurement bias — direct evidence that internal-gap effects are a real, currently uncorrected source of error, not a hypothetical one.
  • lightkurve's own .stitch() (called in fetch_light_curve()) performs its own per-segment normalization when combining quarters/sectors, but this project does not inspect or override that behavior, and does not currently record where the resulting gaps fall in LightCurveData.meta.

Status: PARTIAL. The consequence is real and documented (research log 006) but the fix (explicit gap detection, per-segment detrending, or a quarter-offset correction term) is NOT IMPLEMENTED.

docs.title: 47.4 The real A2 fix as data-quality control — IMPLEMENTED, VALIDATED
docs.text:
Two distinct data-quality problems were found and fixed together (Next Steps A2, docs/NEXT_STEPS.md; also see 59_error_taxonomy.md):

  1. Mixed-cadence stitching. A plain lk.search_lightcurve(target, mission="TESS") could return dozens of products across pipelines (QLP, SPOC, TARS, TASOC, TESS-SPOC, TGLC) at cadences from 20 s to 1800 s. Stitching all of them meant a detrending/baseline window sized in cadences for one cadence was a wildly wrong physical duration at another.
  2. A pipeline-specific flux-normalization corruption. The TARS HLSP pipeline reports flux as an already zero-centered residual rather than raw counts; stitching it in could divide by a near-zero median during normalization, corrupting the result outright (not merely misaligning timestamps).

Both are addressed by the same fix: fetch_light_curve() pins to a single author/exptime (default author="SPOC", exptime=120 for TESS; author="Kepler" for Kepler), which excludes TARS entirely rather than only separating by cadence. Verified against real data: beta Pic resolved to 10 clean SPOC/120s products (down from 54 mixed-pipeline products), with flux normalizing to a "sane 0.99–1.01 range" (Session Log 2026-09-14).

Status: IMPLEMENTED, TESTED (tests/unit/test_cross_cadence.py), VALIDATED against real MAST data.

docs.title: 47.5 Outlier handling — IMPLEMENTED (upward only, by design)
docs.text:
_clip_upper_outliers() in detrend.py replaces flux values more than upper_sigma_clip (5.0) robust-sigma above the median with the median value, before fitting the detrending trend. Downward excursions are never clipped — the docstring is explicit that this is deliberate: "a bright spike is a flare or a cosmic ray, while a faint excursion is the thing we are looking for." The number of points clipped is recorded in meta["detrend_clipped_points"].

Status: IMPLEMENTED. No dedicated unit test file exists for detrend.py at all (Next Steps B7), so this behavior is UNVERIFIED by automated test, though it is straightforward to read directly from source.

docs.title: 47.6 Quality-flag handling (mission pipeline flags) — IMPLEMENTED (default only)
docs.text:
fetch_light_curve() accepts a quality_bitmask parameter (default "default"), passed straight through to lightkurve's own download call — "the default mask removes cadences the mission pipeline flagged as bad" (function docstring). This project does not implement its own quality-flag logic; it relies entirely on lightkurve's interpretation of the mission's own bitmask, at whatever the library's "default" setting currently resolves to. No test in this repository exercises a non-default quality bitmask.

Status: IMPLEMENTED (as a pass-through), UNVERIFIED beyond that.

docs.title: 48. Experiment Registry
docs.text:
Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

Real experiments that have actually run, with commit/config/dataset/outputs traced where recorded. Fields left UNKNOWN were not captured at the time the experiment ran (this project did not have a provenance manifest — see 52_scientific_state_versioning.md). Machine-readable mirror: docs/specification/registry/experiments.yaml.

docs.title: EXP-001 — Six-event KIC 3542116 validation
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-14 through 2026-09-15 (re-run after A1/A4 fixes; exact final re-run timestamp not separately recorded).
  • Description: Re-detect all six published Rappaport et al. (2018) exocomet transit epochs in KIC 3542116 using scripts/run_validation.py / exocomet validate against config/validation_targets.yaml.
  • Commit: UNKNOWN exact commit for the final passing run; current HEAD (01c2051) contains the code that produces this result per the README's own recovery table.
  • Dataset: Real MAST Kepler long-cadence photometry for KIC 3542116 (author="Kepler").
  • Config: config/thresholds.yaml as of the post-A4 state (delta_bic_threshold=10.0, tau_over_sigma_threshold=1.0).
  • Outputs: Console pass/fail table (cmd_validate in cli.py); the specific recovered epochs and depths are recorded in README.md's recovery table (epoch errors 0.029–0.184 d across the six dips).
  • Status: VALIDATED.

docs.title: EXP-002 — B1 depth-offset measurement
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-15.
  • Description: Measured the systematic ~77–78% depth ratio (recovered vs. published) across all six KIC 3542116 dips; tested three hypotheses (baseline contamination H1, fitted-vs-observed depth H2, detrending absorption H3) plus a combined H1+H3, on both a synthetic sanity check and real cached photometry.
  • Commit: Work performed within the 2026-09-15 session (Session Log 2026-09-15 §6); scripts/measure_depth_offset.py (626 lines) is the tool. Exact commit hash for the tool's landing is UNKNOWN from available records; current HEAD contains the script.
  • Dataset: Real, previously cached KIC 3542116 FITS files under data/raw/mastDownload/ (offline mode, --source cache, no network); one known-corrupt cached file (65536-byte truncation) was auto-skipped.
  • Config: Default config/thresholds.yaml at the time; also a baseline-window sweep (2.06 d to 20 d) as a secondary sensitivity test.
  • Outputs: docs/research_log/006-depth-offset-investigation.md, including full per-dip and per-hypothesis ratio tables.
  • Status: VALIDATED as a measurement (the numbers are real and traced); the underlying scientific question (why the residual 10–15% gap exists) remains OPEN — see 49_negative_results.md and 53_threats_to_validity.md.

docs.title: EXP-003 — A4 mirror-image adversarial test
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-15.
  • Description: Generated two synthetic events as exact time-mirrored images of each other (same depth, noise, and total duration; only ingress/egress direction flipped) to test whether ΔBIC alone or τ/σ carries direction information for the flagging decision.
  • Commit: Landed as part of the A4 fix; figure at results/figures/tail_direction.png produced via viz.plots.plot_tail_direction.
  • Dataset: Fully synthetic (not real photometry) — this is a controlled, reproducible unit-test-style experiment, not a survey run.
  • Config: N/A (synthetic construction, not read from thresholds.yaml).
  • Outputs: docs/research_log/007-delta-bic-is-direction-blind.md, with the exact numeric result table (ΔBIC 151 vs 201, τ/σ 4.15 vs 0.23).
  • Status: VALIDATED — this is the evidentiary basis for CLAIM-002 in 43_scientific_claims_registry.md.

docs.title: EXP-004 — Cross-cadence injection-recovery check (A1/A2 fix verification)
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-14.
  • Description: The same synthetic injected comet transit was recovered at matching epoch and τ/σ from both a 120 s-cadence and a 1800 s-cadence version of the same time span, verifying that day-based (not cadence-count-based) window configuration produces cadence-independent results.
  • Commit: Landed alongside the A1/A2 fixes, 2026-09-14.
  • Dataset: Synthetic (no network).
  • Config: Post-A1 config/thresholds.yaml (days-based windows).
  • Outputs: tests/unit/test_cross_cadence.py (a permanent regression test, not a one-off report).
  • Status: TESTED, VALIDATED (runs on every pytest tests/unit invocation).

docs.title: EXP-005 — Real ingestion pipeline end-to-end proof (GitHub Actions)
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-15 (into early 2026-09-16 per commit timestamps).
  • Description: Two escalating real, non-offline test runs against actual MAST data (1 target, then 2 targets, proving resume-after-kill works), followed by a real workflow_dispatch run on GitHub Actions infrastructure (3-minute budget, 1 target), then — after DATA_REPO_TOKEN was added — a full real hourly-cron-shaped run confirmed to push actual output (ledger.jsonl, a Kepler parquet extract, results) into AJpro-merc/exocomet-hunter-data.
  • Commit: afa4bb2 (initial ingest.py + workflow landing), then 01c2051 (current HEAD; control-star matching fix and the confirmed live token-enabled run per Session Log 2026-09-15 §12).
  • Dataset: Real MAST data for KIC 1161345 (single-target test) and the 23 Kepler + 10 TESS hardcoded seed targets thereafter.
  • Config: config/thresholds.yaml at commit 01c2051; ingestion parameters --time-budget-minutes 25, default --max-attempts 3.
  • Outputs: The cloned exocomet-hunter-data repository itself — directly re-verified (2026-09-16): ledger.jsonl contains 33 lines (unique target/mission pairs), 25 with status="success", 8 with status="failed".
  • Status: VALIDATED (the pipeline demonstrably ran and pushed real data successfully at least twice — 2026-09-15 17:50 UTC and 21:07 UTC, per the sibling 23_automation.md section's live gh run list query); continuous unattended operation over time is NOT VALIDATED — the same query shows the two most recent scheduled runs (2026-09-16, 00:05 and 05:50 UTC) both failed on a known, already-locally-fixed-but-uncommitted bug (59_error_taxonomy.md ERR-006; see CLAIM-105 in 43_scientific_claims_registry.md).

docs.title: EXP-006 — KIC 1161345 anomalous flag-rate observation
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-15/16, two independent real MAST fetches.
  • Description: KIC 1161345, assumed "quiet" (part of KEPLER_HOST_STARS), produced 43 flagged candidate events out of roughly 260 detected events across two separate real fetches — an unusually high rate for a supposedly quiet star.
  • Commit: Observed during the scripts/ingest.py real-MAST test runs, 2026-09-15/16.
  • Dataset: Real Kepler long-cadence photometry for KIC 1161345.
  • Config: config/thresholds.yaml at the time of the observation (post-A4).
  • Outputs: A real candidate-record sample from this run is quoted in 76_appendices.md; the star has not yet been run through scripts/vet_host_list.py for a direct verdict.
  • Status: Recorded as an open finding, not yet resolved. See 49_negative_results.md EXP-006 discussion.

docs.title: Injection-recovery / completeness sweeps — STATUS: STALE, not a tracked experiment ID here
docs.text: The README's completeness numbers (50% detection floor near 750 ppm, full recovery above 1000 ppm, from injecting 200 synthetic comets) are explicitly flagged by Next Steps B8 as measured before the A1 (window-units) and A4 (flag-rule) fixes, and not yet regenerated. No experiment ID is assigned here because the run that would need re-doing has not happened yet with the current code; treat the README numbers as historical, not current, per CLAIM-006 in 43_scientific_claims_registry.md.

docs.title: 49. Negative Results
docs.text:
Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

Honest documentation of results that did not confirm a hypothesis, or that surfaced a problem rather than a finding. Per this project's own standing rule, none of the following is called a discovery.

docs.title: 49.1 Unexplained event at BKJD 1064.245 in KIC 3542116
docs.text:
Next Steps B2 records an unexplained excursion at BKJD 1064.245 (531 ppm) in KIC 3542116 — the primary validation star — that is not one of the six published Rappaport et al. (2018) dips. As of this commit, the follow-up checks Next Steps B2 itself specifies have not been run: whether it sits near a quarter boundary or data gap, whether the same timestamp appears in other stars (a spacecraft-wide artefact would), and what its τ/σ and ΔBIC values are.

Status: OPEN, UNVERIFIED. Explicitly not called a discovery — this document repeats that instruction directly from Next Steps B2. It is flagged here specifically so it is not silently forgotten or later mis-cited as a candidate.

docs.title: 49.2 KIC 1161345 — unexpectedly high flag rate on an assumed-quiet host
docs.text:
KIC 1161345 is part of KEPLER_HOST_STARS (scripts/build_kepler_host_list.py), a hand-curated list of stars assumed to be "quiet" (no confirmed planet or eclipsing binary) for use as injection hosts in classifier training. During two independent real MAST fetches in the 2026-09-15/16 scripts/ingest.py test runs, this star produced 43 flagged candidate events out of roughly 260 detected events — consistently across both fetches, i.e. not a one-off fluke of a single run.

This is explicitly compared, in the session record, to KIC 1026032 — a star that was in the same hand-curated list until a direct pipeline run (not a catalog lookup) found a real, strong (~8% deep, ~8.4-day period) periodic signal surviving detrending, almost certainly a genuine eclipsing binary. KIC 1026032 was subsequently moved to KNOWN_BAD_HOSTS. The concern documented here is that KIC 1161345 may be "the same shape of problem" — a hand-curated "quiet" list item that has never actually been checked against a real catalog or a direct pipeline run for suspicious activity.

What has NOT been done: scripts/vet_host_list.py — the tool built specifically to answer "does our own detector find anything suspicious on this star with no injection at all?" — has not yet been run against KIC 1161345. Its module docstring states this is a more directly relevant test than a catalog lookup ("catalog lookups can miss stars nobody ever flagged").

Status: OPEN. Not resolved, not investigated further as of this commit. If KIC 1161345 is a genuine variable/binary and is used as a "clean" injection host in the interim, every noise-class and comet-class training row generated from it before this is resolved should be considered suspect (see 65_false_positive_catalogue.md for how the noise class is generated).

docs.title: 49.3 Model-fit instability on shallow events (H2, surfaced inside B1)
docs.text:
While testing hypothesis H2 (fitted-vs-observed depth) as part of the B1 depth-offset investigation, the comet-model fit was found to diverge badly on at least one shallow event: dip D140 (published depth 491 ppm) was fit at 3.47× its published depth (1704 ppm fitted). The scatter across all six dips under H2 (standard deviation 1.009, essentially as large as the mean 1.316×) confirms this is not an isolated outlier but a real instability affecting the shallow-event regime specifically. Individual per-dip ratios under H2 ranged from 0.99× (D1176, a deep event) to 3.47× (D140, the shallowest).

This was found while investigating a different question (measurement bias in reported depth) and is explicitly logged in docs/research_log/006-depth-offset-investigation.md as "very likely a separate, real bug in detect/model_comparison.py's fit — worth its own investigation." Next Steps lists this as item 4 under "FIRST THING NEXT SESSION," still open as of this commit.

Consequence for other results: if the comet-model fit is unstable on shallow events, the ΔBIC ranking and τ/σ measurement for those same shallow events — the exact quantities the A4 flagging decision (§45.1) depends on — may also be less trustworthy than assumed, independent of the depth-bias question that surfaced it. This is not yet quantified.

Status: OPEN. Not investigated as its own bug as of this commit.

docs.title: 49.4 The depth-offset residual itself is a negative result
docs.text:
Separate from the individual hypotheses, the overall B1 investigation (§48 EXP-002, docs/research_log/006-depth-offset-investigation.md) is itself a negative result worth stating plainly: none of the three tested hypotheses, alone or combined, explains the full ~23% published-vs-recovered depth gap. Combined H1+H3 reaches 87.9% of published depth, 12 percentage points short of unbiased, and the real-data shortfall is larger than what the synthetic sanity check predicted — meaning something specific to real photometry (quarter-stitching offsets are the leading untested suspect) contributes an additional, currently unaccounted-for 10–15%.

Status: OPEN, genuinely unresolved as of this commit. No detector code was changed as a result of this investigation — it was measurement only, by design.

docs.title: 50. Methodological Benchmarking
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 50.1 Current state: NOT IMPLEMENTED
docs.text:
There is no alternative or independent detection method in this codebase to benchmark the asymmetric-dip detector (AsymmetricDipDetector, src/exocomet/detect/comet_detector.py) against. Every result this project currently produces comes from exactly one algorithm. There is consequently no cross-method agreement/disagreement statistic, no comparison table, and no code path that runs two detectors over the same light curve.

This is tracked as Next Steps F3 ("Independent second detector: template matching against a bank of comet profiles; report agreement with the asymmetric-dip detector") and is explicitly framed in Next Steps PART I as one of the higher-leverage gaps: "A second, independent detector... so two different algorithms have to agree — disagreement becomes a signal worth flagging, not noise to average away."

docs.title: 50.2 What F3 would need to exist
docs.text:
• A second Detector subclass (the Detector ABC in core/interfaces.py already exists specifically to make this pluggable — see 57_api_interface_contracts.md) implementing a genuinely different detection method, e.g. matched filtering / template matching against a bank of parametric comet-tail profiles, rather than the current threshold-plus-model-comparison approach.
  • A shared evaluation harness that runs both detectors over the same light curve set (at minimum the validation targets in config/validation_targets.yaml, ideally also the injection-recovery grid in calibration/injection.py) and reports per-event agreement/disagreement, not just aggregate recall.
  • A defined policy for what disagreement means for the flagged decision — Next Steps PART I is explicit that disagreement should become "a signal worth flagging, not noise to average away," which implies a new field on CandidateRecord or EventScore rather than silently picking one detector's answer.
  • A comparison against the one external precedent this project's own README cites — Kennedy et al. (2019), MNRAS 482, 5587, "An automated search for transiting exocomets" — would be the natural literature benchmark, but note that comparing against a paper's reported results is not the same as running that paper's actual code; no such independent codebase is vendored or referenced here.

Status: PLANNED, NOT IMPLEMENTED. No implementation, test, or partial scaffold for F3 was found anywhere in the repository.

docs.title: 51. Pipeline Observability
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 51.1 What exists today
docs.text:
Stdout/log progress. scripts/ingest.py::run_ingest() logs, via the standard logging module (INFO level, configured at module import), a per-mission summary line before processing ("N target(s) total, N pending, N queued this run") and a per-target outcome line on success or failure. main() prints a final one-line summary: "{mission}: {succeeded} succeeded, {failed} failed, {skipped_budget} left for next run". This is real, human-readable console output — visible directly in GitHub Actions' own log viewer for each run — but is not aggregated, alerted on, or queryable outside of reading raw logs.

The ledger as an observability artifact. io/ledger.py's append-only JSONL ledger (ledger.jsonl in the data repo) is, incidentally, the closest thing this project has to a durable operational record: every attempt at every target, with timestamp, status, attempt count, and error message on failure. It was read directly (docs/specification/48_experiment_registry.md EXP-005) to get real, current success/failure counts (33 unique targets: 25 succeeded, 8 failed, as of 2026-09-16) — this works, but only because someone clones the repo and greps/parses it by hand or via scripts/build_local_db.py.

scripts/build_local_db.py. Rebuilds a disposable local SQLite view (local.db) from the ledger on demand, with three tables: attempts (full retry history), targets (latest status per star, including n_candidates/n_flagged computed by reading each results file, correctly distinguishing NULL — never processed/failed — from 0 — processed, zero candidates), and candidates (one row per detected event, across all stars, so "show every flagged candidate" is one query instead of opening N files). This is a genuine, tested local observability tool, but it must be run manually; nothing regenerates or serves it automatically.

GitHub Actions' own pass/fail UI. Each workflow run (ingest.yml, train.yml, survey.yml) shows up in GitHub's own Actions tab with a per-job/per-step pass/fail status and the raw log output. This is real and does not require any code in this repository — it is GitHub's own product surface, not something this project built.

survey.yml's job summary. The (currently disabled) survey.yml workflow writes a short markdown summary to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY (candidate count on record) on every run, visible in the Actions UI. This is the one place in the repository that writes a structured "summary" artifact at all, and it applies only to the disabled legacy survey workflow, not to ingest.yml.

docs.title: 51.2 What does NOT exist
docs.text:
• No alerting. Nothing pages, emails, or otherwise notifies anyone when a run fails, when the ingestion pipeline stalls, or when an anomaly like the KIC 1161345 flag-rate spike (49_negative_results.md §49.2) occurs. Discovery of that anomaly happened because a human was watching a live test run, not because any monitoring surfaced it.
  • No dashboards. There is no web UI, no Grafana/similar panel, and no scheduled report beyond GitHub Actions' own per-run UI. Next Steps J10 ("live 'stars currently being analysed' counter") is explicitly proposed and explicitly not yet built, gated on the six-event validation exam being reliably green first.
  • No health-check endpoint. Nothing exposes "is the pipeline currently healthy" as a queryable signal; the only way to know is to read the ledger or the Actions log by hand.
  • No metrics/telemetry pipeline. No timing, memory, or throughput metrics are emitted anywhere outside of what is documented in 70_performance_benchmarking.md (a handful of numbers recorded in session logs, not instrumented in code).
  • No structured run manifest. scripts/train_classifier.py writes an append-only manifest (models/manifest_<mission>.jsonl) for training runs specifically, but no equivalent exists for detection/ingestion runs — see 52_scientific_state_versioning.md for how this compares to the Next Steps E3 provenance-manifest proposal.

docs.title: 51.3 A note on conflicting operational records — resolved with real live data
docs.text:
docs/NEXT_STEPS.md's own "FIRST THING NEXT SESSION" section (near the top of the file) lists "Set up DATA_REPO_TOKEN" as an outstanding first step, while a later section of the same document's linked Session Log (Session Log 2026-09-15.md §12, "DATA_REPO_TOKEN added, automation confirmed fully live") states the token was added and a live run was confirmed. 23_automation.md independently resolves this by querying GitHub directly (gh workflow list --all, gh run list, 2026-09-16): ingest is confirmed active, and survey/train are both confirmed disabled_manually — corroborating §12's account over the stale "FIRST THING" list.

That same live query surfaces a real, current operational problem this section's earlier draft could not see: the two most recent scheduled ingest runs (2026-09-16T00:05:07Z and 2026-09-16T05:50:28Z, roughly six hours apart) both failed, in about a minute each — short and fast, consistent with the run exhausting its target budget on unresolvable identifiers rather than a network stall. Root cause (per 59_error_taxonomy.md ERR-006): five hardcoded Kepler IDs with no real MAST observations, which the committed code (01c2051) retries as ordinary failures rather than recording as permanently unresolvable; a fix for this exists only in the local working tree as of this writing and has not been committed or pushed. Two earlier runs on 2026-09-15 (17:50 workflow_dispatch, 21:07 schedule, both success) show the pipeline has previously completed end-to-end — the 2026-09-16 failures are a regression against a known, already-diagnosed, not-yet-shipped bug, not evidence the pipeline has never worked.

This is itself direct evidence for the observability gap described in §51.2: nobody was alerted to these two live failures; they were found only because this document and 23_automation.md went and queried GitHub Actions directly. A pipeline with real alerting would not have let two consecutive scheduled failures pass unnoticed for at least six hours.

docs.title: 52. Scientific State Versioning
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 52.1 What is captured today
docs.text:
• Git commit, via CI checkout. Every GitHub Actions run checks out a specific commit (actions/checkout@v4), so in principle the exact code version that produced a given ingestion or training run is recoverable from the run's own log — but only if that log is still retained by GitHub and someone goes and looks. Nothing in the pipeline's own output (ledger entries, results files) records the git commit SHA that produced them.
  • The config file as committed alongside code. config/thresholds.yaml is versioned in the same repository and commit history as the detection code that reads it, so git log -p config/thresholds.yaml gives a real, if manual, history of parameter changes. PipelineConfig.to_dict() (core/config.py) can serialize the full resolved configuration, but nothing currently calls this and writes the result alongside a run's output.
  • scripts/train_classifier.py's provenance manifest. This is the one place in the codebase with a real, append-only provenance record: models/manifest_<mission>.jsonl records row count, class counts, host stars used, date, package versions, and a training-set hash for every training run (Next Steps C2). This is a genuine partial implementation of the general idea, scoped narrowly to model training.
  • The ledger's timestamp field. Every LedgerEntry (io/ledger.py) carries timestamp_utc, giving a real per-attempt time record, though not a code-version or config-version record.

docs.title: 52.2 What is NOT captured (Next Steps E3 — NOT IMPLEMENTED)
docs.text:
Next Steps E3 specifies a full provenance manifest: every run writes results/runs/<timestamp>.json with config, package version, git commit, Python/OS, seed, target-list hash, lightkurve author/exptime, and output checksums. No such file, function, or code path exists anywhere in the repository as of this commit. Specifically missing, compared to the training manifest that does exist:

  • No git commit SHA recorded per detection/ingestion run (only per training run, and even there, only implicitly via when the manifest line was written).
  • No Python/OS/package-version snapshot for detection runs (train_classifier.py's manifest records package versions for training specifically, not for scripts/ingest.py).
  • No target-list hash — if config/target_list_kepler.txt or watchlist.txt changes between two runs, nothing records which version was used for which output.
  • No output checksums anywhere.
  • No single results/runs/<timestamp>.json file format defined or written by any script.

docs.title: 52.3 Specification versioning
docs.text: This document (EHS-CTS) is itself the first version of a specification for this project, with no prior version to diff against (per 00_document_control.md). No spec-versioning scheme beyond "v1.0, dated 2026-09-16" exists. Sections 43–76, the registry, and the infrastructure files described here are part of that v1.0; the overall document's future versioning policy (how a v1.1 would be produced, what triggers a version bump) is itself NOT yet defined anywhere in the repository — see 62_release_and_versioning.md.

docs.title: 52.4 Consequence
docs.text:
Because no run-level provenance manifest exists, a specific number appearing in results/Kepler/KIC_1161345.jsonl today cannot currently be traced back to the exact commit, config, or package versions that produced it without manually cross-referencing timestamps against git log and the session logs by hand — exactly the kind of manual reconciliation this specification project itself has had to do to write §52.1 above. This is a genuine, acknowledged gap, not a hypothetical one.

Status: PARTIAL (training manifest exists; general run provenance, NOT IMPLEMENTED).

docs.title: 53. Threats to Validity
docs.text:
Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

Organized by the standard four-way split. Each item cites its concrete evidence rather than asserting the threat abstractly.

docs.title: 53.1 Internal validity
docs.text:
The unexplained ~12–15% residual depth bias. Even after correcting for the two mechanisms actually tested (baseline contamination H1, detrending absorption H3 — H3 ruled out, H1 real but partial), measured event depths in KIC 3542116 remain roughly 12 percentage points below an unbiased estimate on real data, and the real-data shortfall is larger than what the same test predicted on synthetic data (docs/research_log/006-depth-offset-investigation.md). This means some property specific to real photometry — quarter-stitching offsets are the leading untested suspect — is influencing the measurement in a way the current pipeline does not correct for. Any depth-dependent conclusion (e.g. a completeness curve, a claimed detection floor) inherits this uncertainty.

The comet-model fit's instability on shallow events (§49.3). A model that diverges to 3.47× the true depth on at least one real shallow event calls into question the reliability of ΔBIC and τ/σ — the exact two quantities the flagging decision depends on (§45.1) — specifically in the shallow-event regime, independent of the depth-bias question that surfaced it.

docs.title: 53.2 External (generalizability) validity
docs.text:
Mission/cadence dependence — the A1/A2 story. The entire A1 (day-based vs. cadence-based window sizing) and A2 (pinning TESS to a single author/exptime) fix history exists because the pipeline's behavior was, before those fixes, silently wrong when applied to TESS cadences after being tuned against Kepler's 29.4-minute cadence. The fix is validated for the specific case tested (tests/unit/test_cross_cadence.py, beta Pic at 120s vs 1800s), but this is evidence the pipeline generalizes across the tested cadence range, not proof it generalizes to every mission/cadence/pipeline combination MAST can return (e.g. TESS 20-second ultra-short cadence, or K2's variable-length campaigns, are not covered by any test found in this repository).

Host-star selection is not representative by construction. KEPLER_HOST_STARS is a hand-curated ~18-star list explicitly chosen as "quiet" candidates, not a random or catalog-driven sample; config/watchlist.txt/tess_training_hosts.txt are explicitly astrophysically-motivated debris-disc/exocomet-precedent stars, not a control sample. scripts/build_target_list.py's catalogue-driven expansion (which would include a genuinely matched control group, Next Steps E6/F4) has a real, acknowledged gap: its control-star matching returns zero matches for all 5 tested disc hosts (Session Log 2026-09-15 §11), so it is not wired into ingest.py. Any population-level claim ("debris-disc stars show more candidates than control stars") is therefore currently impossible to make with this codebase's actual data.

docs.title: 53.3 Statistical validity
docs.text:
Trials factor / look-elsewhere effect — not measured. Per-event significance (ΔBIC, τ/σ, the bootstrap-derived a_dur_sigma) does not account for how many places were searched — how many stars, how many candidate windows per star, how many configuration variants were tried during development. The README's own "Honest limitations" section states this directly. Next Steps D5/J2 propose an empirical look-elsewhere correction (running the detector over ~10,000 quiet or time-reversed light curves and reporting "N candidates per 10,000 null curves at this threshold") specifically because a formal p-value cannot yet be justified; this is PLANNED, not measured, as of this commit (see 69_statistical_methodology.md).

No formal power/false-positive-rate characterization against the seven implemented lookalike classes. calibration/injection.py + scripts/generate_training_labels.py implement seven injection classes (comet, symmetric, reversed, flare, starspot, noise, time_reversed_real) for classifier training, but Next Steps D1's proposed confusion matrix ("what fraction of each lookalike gets called a comet" by the current rule-based flagging decision, independent of the not-yet-trained classifier) has not been produced — see 65_false_positive_catalogue.md.

docs.title: 53.4 Construct validity
docs.text:
Does asymmetry alone imply a comet? No — and this project has direct, documented evidence of the failure mode that results from assuming so. docs/research_log/007-delta-bic-is-direction-blind.md shows a synthetic physically backwards (leading-tail, i.e. the wrong direction for a trailing dust tail) event scoring a higher ΔBIC (201) than the genuine trailing-tail comet shape (151). ΔBIC measures "is this asymmetric," not "is this asymmetric in the physically correct direction for a comet." Only τ/σ (4.15 vs. 0.23) distinguishes the two. This is why the A4 flagging rule requires both conditions (§45.1), and why the research log itself carries an explicit warning against ever "simplifying" the rule by dropping the τ/σ term — doing so would silently reintroduce exactly this construct-validity failure while still passing the six-event validation exam (since the six known dips are genuine trailing-tail events and satisfy either rule).

"Flagged" is not "candidate is real," and "candidate" is not "confirmed." The type system enforces a VettingStatus.CANDIDATE as the strongest available positive status (core/types.py), and this document's own vocabulary rule (§0.4 of 00_document_control.md) forbids the word "confirmed" for any detection. This is a construct-validity guard maintained by convention and documentation discipline, not by a runtime check (§44.1, REQ-VALID-003) — there is nothing in code that would prevent a future contributor from writing "confirmed exocomet" into a script's output, and this specification project itself is one of the few artifacts actively enforcing the distinction in writing.

No pixel-level check that a dimming signal actually originates from the target star. src/exocomet/vetting/ is empty (§45.5). A background eclipsing binary bleeding into the photometric aperture would currently be indistinguishable, in this pipeline's own output, from a genuine target-star dimming event with the right asymmetric shape. Both external reviews cited in Next Steps J1 independently rank this the single biggest missing capability, and this document agrees it is a construct-validity threat, not merely a missing feature: it means "candidate" currently means "an asymmetric dip was measured somewhere in this aperture," not "an asymmetric dip on this star."

docs.title: 54. Automated Scientific Reasoning
docs.text: Status: reflects repo state as of 2026-09-16, commit 01c2051.

docs.title: 54.1 H1 — the planned AI-skeptic review layer (PLANNED, NOT IMPLEMENTED)
docs.text:
Next Steps H1 specifies a design for an AI review layer (originally scoped to a free-tier Gemini model): it would receive only computed features as JSON — never a light curve, never raw data — and return structured JSON output: evidence for, evidence against, alternative explanations, and a recommended next test. It must be able to answer insufficient_evidence, and the load-bearing design rule, stated explicitly in Next Steps, is:

The model never decides whether something is a comet. ... Use it as a skeptic, not a cheerleader.

Next Steps PART I sharpens this further, proposing the review be explicitly prompted to disprove the candidate rather than confirm it, and lists the hard guardrails: it may summarize, critique, propose alternative explanations, and suggest next tests; it may never alter a measurement, compute an authoritative statistic, silently change a label, or claim a discovery.

No code implementing any part of this exists in the repository as of this commit. No API call to any LLM provider, no prompt template, no JSON schema for the feature payload or the response, and no integration point in core/interfaces.py or elsewhere reserves a place for this layer. It remains a written design, not a partial build.

Status: PLANNED, NOT IMPLEMENTED.

docs.title: 54.2 The broader "falsification engine" concept (Next Steps PART I) — PLANNED, NOT IMPLEMENTED
docs.text: The external-review-derived roadmap in Next Steps PART I proposes running every candidate through an automatic battery of disprove-it tests (eclipsing-binary check, flare morphology, starspot fit, instrumental-artefact check, sector-edge proximity, periodicity, detrending-method sensitivity, cross-sector persistence) reported as PASS/FAIL per test rather than a single confidence number. This overlaps heavily with the planned vetting/checks.py module (Next Steps D2, §45.5) and is likewise entirely unbuilt — src/exocomet/vetting/ contains only a docstring.

docs.title: 54.3 Contrast: what "automated scientific reasoning" does NOT mean in this project
docs.text: To avoid the vocabulary drifting: nothing in this codebase today uses a machine-learning model, an LLM, or any automated system to decide that a candidate is or is not an exocomet. The one place a trained classifier is planned (Next Steps PART C, scripts/train_classifier.py) is explicitly designed to produce a comet_probability score — a reported column, subject to the same "candidate, never confirmed" vocabulary rule as everything else (§45.1, §53.4) — not an autonomous accept/reject decision, and per Next Steps C4 it is meant to sit alongside the physics-based A4 rule as a comparison, not a silent replacement.

docs.title: 55.5 What this means for the README's "Data sources" claim
docs.text: README.md states light-curve data comes from MAST and cross-match data comes from "the NASA Exoplanet Archive, VizieR, SIMBAD and the Gaia archive." Based on direct code inspection: MAST and VizieR are real, live, and exercised. NASA Exoplanet Archive is referenced only as the rationale for a hand-curated list, not queried live. SIMBAD and Gaia are not queried by any code found in this repository. This is not a contradiction so much as a forward-looking README describing the intended final data-source set for the (currently empty) vetting/ module alongside what is already real; a reader should not assume every source named in the README is currently exercised by running code.

docs.title: 56.2 scripts/ingest.py per-target data flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Ingest as scripts/ingest.py
    participant MAST as MAST (via lightkurve)
    participant Extract as io/extract.py
    participant Detect as detrend + detect
    participant Ledger as io/ledger.py

    Ingest->>MAST: fetch_light_curve(target_id, mission)
    MAST-->>Ingest: LightCurveData (raw FITS still on local disk)
    Ingest->>Extract: save_extract(lc, extract_path)  [atomic, os.replace]

Source: scripts/ingest.py::process_one_target() module and function docstrings, verified against the actual step-by-step code (steps 1–6 numbered explicitly in the source).
